name: Muir
history_scottish:
King makers

Some believe that the Muir Clan can trace its origin right back to the starting point of Scotland as a nation. For years it was thought the Scottish Gaels originated from the Dal Riata tribe in Antrim, in Northern Ireland. At around 500 AD Fergus Mor mac Eirc was forced out of his Antrim home and invaded Argyll where he established a new Dal Riata by kicking out the Picts who were already living there.

This was the start of a chain of events which culminated with the Gaels taking over the Pictish nation and creating a unified kingdom of Alba in the ninth century. Eventually Alba evolved into the Scotland we know and love today. It’s thought that for many centuries the Muirs subscribed to this theory, believing their name originated from Mor. Indeed, a seventeenth century book written by Sir William Mure states that the idea they originated from the ancient Irish tribe of O’More was generally accepted within the family at that time. However, in the late twentieth century archeologists began to doubt the evidence. Now, there are strong grounds for concluding that the Gaels did not invade Scotland at that time. Nevertheless, the Muir clan, often known as Mure, More and Moore, played a major role in the formation of the UK’s Royal families, north and south of the Border.

The turning point which saw them rise from relative obscurity to king-makers began with the Battle of Largs and the brave exploits of Gilchrist Muir. King Hakon of Norway, worried about another Scottish attempt to wrest Argyll and the isles from his control decided on a pre-emptive strike. In July 1263 he left the port of Bergen with 200 ships and by the time he reached the western isles of Scotland his forces had been swelled further. Hakon attacked the mainland with initial success before the Scots began negotiating with him. This was a delaying tactic to enable them to mobilise their forces. During the talks a major storm erupted just off Largs. This forced the Norwegians to attempt to shelter on dry land. The combination of terrible weather and difficult terrain left them wide open to attack and they were unable to re-organise themselves into a fighting force. Consequently the Norsemen suffered a heavy defeat. The Scots were led into battle by Gilchrist Muir and chased the invaders into the sea amid much slaughter. A grateful King Alexander III knighted Muir and gave him the lands of Rowallan near Kilmarnock. He built a tower there and married Isobel the daughter of Sir Walter Cumyn, a powerful landowner nearby with whom he’d previously fallen out. When Cumyn died Sir Gilchrist inherited Sir Walter’s land not only in and around Rowallan but also in Roxburghshire in the Borders. Sir Gilchrist died in 1280, at the age of 80. He had two daughters, Elizabeth and Anicia. The latter married Richard Boyle of Kelburn, anscestor of the Earls of Glasgow, who still own the Kelburn estate near Largs. Sir Gilchrist’s son, Archibald, died in the Battle of Berwick in 1297. Archibald’s grandson, Adam, had two sons and a daughter, also Elizabeth, who was described as being of great beauty and rare virtue. In 1336 Elizabeth Muir married Robert Stewart, the grandson of Robert the Bruce and nephew of King David II of Scotland. He was born in 1316 and was a grandson of Robert the Bruce. His mother, Marjorie, was the Bruce’s daughter. His father was Walter the sixth High Steward of Scotland. Robert took his father’s position as his surname and therefore became the first of the line of Stewart or Stuart kings, who in 1603 also became kings of England. King David was on the throne of Scotland at the time of the wedding but he became an absent monarch. He had invaded England in 1346 but was captured at the Battle of Neville’s Cross, remaining a prisoner at the English court until the Treaty of Berwick in 1357. He was returned to Scotland on payment of a large ransom. In his absence Robert Stewart became the Governor of a Scotland on the brink of civil war. With the king away rival nobles were jockeying for position and armed confrontations were commonplace. The Black Death was rampaging through the population reducing it by more than a quarter. Despite these great pressures Robert quietly and shrewdly built up his power base. David was released in 1357 and when he died without children in 1371 Robert succeeded him. Elizabeth had died in 1355 and so never became queen. She had initially become his mistress. Their marriage was criticised as uncanonical, so in 1349 following a Papal Dispensation they remarried. Their children, uniquely, played a substantial role in the formation of two British Royal families, the House of Stuart and the Hanoverians who followed them. Their direct male heirs ruled Scotland until James V died in 1542. James V’s daughter, Mary, Queen of Scots, then took the reins. Her son, James VI of Scotland then became James I of England. Their descendants ruled both countries until 1714 when Queen Anne died. At that point the Hanoverians from Germany took over and today they still rule the United Kingdom. Elizabeth Mure had several daughters. One of them, Jean Stewart, married Sir John Lyon. Their children became the Earls of Strathmore and Kinghorne. Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon is a direct descendant of the fourteenth Earl. In 1923 she married Albert, the Duke of York, the second son of King George V and Queen Mary. As Duchess of York she became known as the “Smiling Duchess” because of her consistent public expression. In 1936, her husband unexpectedly became King when her brother-in-law, Edward VIII, abdicated in order to marry his mistress, the American divorcée Wallis Simpson. Her daughter Elizabeth II is the reigning Hanoverian monarch.

King Robert II and Elizabeth Muir had several sons. Their first was John Stewart who went on to become King Robert III in 1390 after his father died. One of his brothers became the notorious Wolf of Badenoch. This was Alexander Stewart, the fourth, and youngest, son of Robert and Elizabeth. Alexander is infamously remembered for his sacking of Elgin and its cathedral. His nickname was earned due to his outrageous cruelty. In May 1390, after a feud with Bishop Alexander Bur of Moray, Alexander Stewart, by now the Earl of Buchan, burned the Royal Burgh of Forres and the Church of St Lawrence. The following month he burned a large part of Elgin including the cathedral, a monastery, churches and a hospital. Buchan disliked Bishop Bur because the churchman had helped the Earl’s wife, Euphemia the Countess of Ross, successfully file for divorce. The couple had no children but the Earl fathered several with his mistress, Mairead Inghean Eachann, including Alexander Stewart who became the Earl of Mar. As a consequence of the divorce Buchan lost a great deal of land which had previously belonged to his wife and now reverted back to her. Buchan died in 1405 and is buried in Dunkeld Cathedral. His armour-covered tomb is one of the few Scottish royal monuments to have survived from the Middle Ages.

There were other strands of the Muir Clan dotted around Scotland in the thirteenth century and a number of them including Gilchrist Muir were of high enough stature to be signatories on the Ragman’s Roll. This was a record of the acts of fealty and homage which King Edward I of England forced Scotland’s nobility and gentry to sign in 1296. Edward was known as The Hammer of the Scots because of his attempts to impose his rule on the land north of the border. Initially, Edward had planned to annex Scotland through marriage. His intention was for his son and heir Edward to marry Margaret the Maid of Norway. She was the daughter of King Eirik II of Norway and Margaret, daughter of King Alexander III of Scotland. The princess was born in 1283 and was sometimes known as Margaret of Scotland and was considered to have been Queen of Scots from 1286 until she died in 1290 with no successor. There were fears that without a clear-cut heir to the Scottish throne a power vacuum would develop and the country would descend into tribal war. In order to prevent this Edward was invited by the nobility and other power brokers of the time to rule on who would be the next king. In return he insisted on the signatures to the Ragman Roll. The Muirs who added their names to it were The Mores of Levenaches’ Adam de More of Ayrshire, Reginald de More of Ayrshire, Gilchrist Muir of Ayrshire, Reynauld Mor of Cragg, Lanarkshire and Symon de la Moore of Thankerton. The list illustrates the variation in the spelling of the surname.

Troubled times

A number of Muirs joined the Covenanters. These were Scots who would not accept that King Charles I was head of the church. They signed a covenant which stated that only Jesus Christ could hold that position.

King Charles inherited the throne in 1625. His father James VI of Scotland became James I of England in March 1603. Scotland’s religion was Presbyterianism, a harsh strict form of Protestantism. King James believed that his rule had a higher authority than the church’s. Despite that he failed in his attempts to force the Scots to embrace his Episcopalian doctrine, which allowed the monarch to appoint bishops to the church. King Charles, who was born in Fife, decided to finish his father’s job. In 1637 he ordered that the Book of Common Prayer should be read in St Giles Cathedral, Edinburgh. The congregation was furious. Many believed it was closer to Catholicism than Protestantism. Seven months later, in February 1638, Scotland’s National Covenant was published. This document, prepared with the full support of the nobility and land-owning class, proclaimed Scotland’s opposition to the king’s new prayer book. It was put on public view in Edinburgh and immediately attracted 60,000 signatures. Copies were taken throughout the country and many more signed up. In 1642 the First English Civil War erupted, between Charles and the forces loyal to his former Parliament, which he had tried to dismiss. The Covenanters allied themselves with the Parliamentarians, known as the Roundheads, who were led by Oliver Cromwell. By May 1646 The Royalists were defeated and Charles surrendered to the Scots. While imprisoned he convinced the Covenanters to switch their allegiance to him in return for a promise to make England a Presbyterian state. Soon after, the Covenanters invaded England in the hope of restoring Charles to the throne. This was the start of the Second English Civil War. But they were no match for Cromwell’s battle-hardened New Model Army and were heavily defeated after a series of battles. When the dust settled Charles was executed by public beheading in January 1649 and Cromwell governed the country. In 1660 the Monarchy was restored and King Charles II was welcomed back to England from exile on the Continent. A year later Banffshire-born James Sharp was appointed Archbishop of St Andrews and immediately began a drive to bring episcopacy to Scotland coupled with a brutal repression of Presbyterianism. Some Covenanters were also signatories of the Apologetical Declaration which declared war on all established political officials, soldiers, judges, conformist ministers, and informers. This document, however, provoked vicious reprisals by the authorities and the period became known as the Killing Times. During 1684-85, at least 78 Covenanters were executed without trial for refusing to retract their allegiance to the declaration, while others were executed after a show trial. Among them was James Muir, who was hanged for his beliefs on February 22, 1684 in Edinburgh.

name: Murdoch
history_scottish:
Fields of battle

A name with ancient Celtic roots, ‘Murdoch’ is ranked at 97 in the list of the 100 most popular surnames in Scotland.

Not exclusive to any particular region, it was to be found from earliest times from Galloway in the southwest to the Western Isles and in Badenoch, Strathspey.

Also a popular forename in the form of ‘Murdo’, it is thought to derive from the Gaelic muireach, indicating ‘mariner’ or murchadh, meaning ‘sea warrior’.

In Ireland, ‘Murdoch’ and ‘Murdock’ are anglicised forms of the native Irish Gaelic Ó Muircheartaigh – although Protestant settlers also brought the names to the island from Scotland in the seventeenth century.

Although heirs to their own proud traditions, the Murdochs of today are also recognised as a sept, or sub-branch, of two renowned Scottish clans – those of Clan Macpherson and Clan MacDonald – more properly known as Clan Donald – and, as such, entitled to wear their tartans.

As a sept of Clan Donald – one of Scotland’s largest clans and whose several branches include the MacDonalds of Sleat, Clanranald, Glengarry and Keppoch – the Murdochs shared in both their fortunes and misfortunes.

With their motto of ‘By sea, by land’, and crest of an armoured hand holding a cross, the MacDonalds were masters of a sprawling fiefdom, ruling a confederacy of clans while, from their base at Dunyveg on the south of Islay, they controlled a strategic sea route between the north of Ireland and Scotland’s western seaboard.

Of Norse-Gaelic roots, the clan takes its name from Donald, 1st Lord of the Isles, and a grandson of the twelfth century Somerled.

By the mid-twelfth century, Somerled, or Somhairle, whose name means ‘summer wanderer’ or ‘summer sailor’, had carved out a vast west coast fiefdom that included the south isles from Bute to Ardnamurchan Point in addition to Kintyre, Argyll and Lorne.

Known as the King of the Isles and fiercely independent, he considered he owed allegiance to no man, not least the King of Scots.

It was following the death of David I in 1153 that his grandson, Malcolm, succeeded to the throne as Malcolm IV.

He inherited a troubled kingdom torn apart by not only internecine warfare on the mainland but the threat of invasion from the north by Vikings, who sacked Aberdeen in the same year that he succeeded to the throne, and invasion from the west in the form of Somerled.

A powerful group of ambitious magnates, mainly centred in the Moray area in the northeast of Scotland, resolved to depose Malcolm, replacing him with their own puppet king, and were joined in this bold venture by Somerled.

In 1157, one year after he defeated his wife’s brother, Godfred, the King of Man, in a sea battle off Islay, in the Inner Hebrides, Somerled seized control of the islands of Bute and Arran.

Control of these strategically important islands increased the threat he posed to the west coast mainland and Malcolm, rather naively, sought to resolve the problem by ordering Somerled to surrender his domains into the hands of the Crown, thereafter holding them as a mere vassal.

Somerled’s answer was predictable.

He assembled a 15,000 strong force of kinsmen and, embarking in a fleet of 164 swift galleys, sailed up the Firth of Clyde and then up the Clyde to sack the town of Glasgow in a blood-crazed orgy of arson, rape and plunder.

Malcolm’s loyal magnate in the west, Walter Fitzalan, the High Steward, hastily assembled a rag-tag force of other loyal magnates and their retainers.

Somerled, eager to face the challenge, met the woefully inadequate royal army at Renfrew.

Accounts differ on what now actually transpired on that bitterly cold day of January 1st, 1164.

One account is that a fierce battle ensued and, as Somerled’s battle-hardened Islesmen rapidly gained the upper hand over the royal forces, the tide of battle turned when Somerled received a mortal thrust from a spear.

Dismayed at the loss of their leader, the Islesmen’s discipline broke down, and hundreds were slaughtered as they fled back to their galleys.

A rather less heroic account of the victory, however, is that the High Steward had realised he had no realistic hope of defeating Somerled in a set-piece battle and, accordingly, bribed Maurice MacNeill, Somerled’s nephew, to murder his uncle.

MacNeill accomplished this treacherous deed by gaining admittance to Somerled’s tent after his army had encamped at Renfrew and stabbed him through the heart, possibly while he slept.

Donald, grandson of Somerled, died in about 1250, and his descendants were stalwart in their support of Scotland’s great warrior king Robert the Bruce, with Angus Og MacDonald and his kinsfolk fighting at his side at the battle of Bannockburn.

This was in June of 1314, when a 20,000-strong English army under Edward II was defeated by a Scots army less than half this strength.

It was as reward for Clan Donald’s loyal support that Bruce rewarded them by proclaiming that, in future battles, they would be given the honoured position of fighting on the right wing of the Scots army.

Nearly 200 years later, in September of 1513, Clan Donald and their kinsfolk such as the Murdochs were on the bloody field of battle known as Flodden.

This was a truly national disaster, with an estimated 10,000 Scots who included James IV, an archbishop, two bishops, eleven earls, fifteen barons and 300 knights killed.

The clan also proved loyal to the cause of the Royal House of Stuart, supporting it throughout the abortive Jacobite Risings of 1715 and 1745.

Bearers of the Murdoch name also fought for the Stuart cause through their kinship with Clan Macpherson.

With their main territory in Badenoch, in Strathspey, and with their motto of ‘Touch not the cat without a glove’ and crest of a rampant wildcat, this ancient clan were also leading members of the powerful confederation of clans known as Clan Chattan.

It was Ewen Macpherson, Chief of the Macphersons, who led his clansmen and kinsmen such as the Murdochs at Culloden. Following the defeat, and with a price on his head, he spent nine long years hiding out in the rugged grandeur of Badenoch before being able to escape to France.

In addition to their close affiliation to Clan Donald of the Western Isles and Clan Macpherson of Badenoch, bearers of the Murdoch name also have a strong association with Galloway – to the extent that it explains a rather odd central motif that appears on some Murdoch Coats of Arms.

This is a motif of two ravens pierced, or transfixed, through the heads by an arrow.

The origins of this go back to the early months of 1307 when Robert the Bruce, who had been enthroned as King of Scots only about a year earlier, found himself a hunted man, closely pursued through Galloway by his enemies.

It was a time when the fortunes of the great warrior king were at one of their lowest ebbs, and it was only because of the selfless support he received from others that he was able to rally his fortunes and, seven years later, achieve his great victory at Bannockburn.

Those who rallied to his cause, even when it appeared hopeless, included a widow woman and her three sons from Craigencallie, near Loch Dee.

The widow sheltered the fugitive king in her cottage, offering him some humble but nevertheless welcome fare, before introducing him to her sons.

Eager to impress their king, one of the lads demonstrated his astonishing archery skills by, firing only one arrow, shooting two ravens perched on a rock, both through the head. Impressed by his skill with the bow, Bruce invited him and his two brothers to join his then meagre forces.

The lads are reputed to have subsequently served him through thick and thin, ultimately being rewarded with the lands of Hassock and Cumloden, northwest of Newton Stewart, in Galloway.

It was here, known as the Murdochs of Cumloden, that the family held lands up until about the middle of the eighteenth century – with a Coat of Arms featuring two ravens transfixed through the heads by an arrow.

Poetry and the press

Far from the fields of battle and recognised as having played a profound role in the educational development of Scotland’s national bard Robert Burns, John Murdoch was born in Ayrshire in 1747. His influence on Burns cannot be overestimated.

It was in May of 1765 that Murdoch, then a 19-year-old student of languages, was approached by Burns’ father, William, to provide educational instruction for his sons Robert and Gilbert and also for other children from the small Ayrshire village of Alloway.

With his salary paid by the parents of his young charges and their families taking it in turn to lodge and feed him, Murdoch eagerly embarked on an educational regime that taught the basics of education before introducing the study of literary English and the Old and the New Testament.

Burns, aged six when he first came under Murdoch’s tutelage, thrived under the young schoolteacher’s guidance, and his poetic imagination was fired when he introduced him to Arthur Masson’s A Collection of Prose and Verse, from the Best English Authors.

The future national bard’s full-time schooling under Murdoch ended after only two and a half years, when the teacher was appointed to a post at a school in Ayr.

But Murdoch still found time to visit the Burns household and devote time to the budding poet, frequently gifting him inspirational works of literature.

Never afraid to speak his mind, Murdoch lost his teaching position in Ayr after expressing controversial views over a locally prominent and influential minister of the Church of Scotland.

Leaving his native Scotland, he settled in London, eking out a meagre living as a language teacher and seller of stationery.

He and Burns maintained a regular correspondence up until the poet’s early death in Dumfries in July of 1796. Murdoch survived him by 28 years, dying in extreme poverty in London in 1824.

Bearers of the Murdoch name have also imprinted their mark on the historical record through endeavours far from the land of their birth.

Born in 1850 in Paisley, George Murdoch was aged five when he left Scotland with his family to settle in Saint John, New Brunswick.

Moving to Calgary at the age of 23 and starting a successful horse harness business, he is recognised today as having been the city of Calgary’s first permanent businessman.

The main clientele for his harness equipment were the North West Mounted Police and the Blackfoot Indians, whose language he was able to master.

Serving from 1884 to 1886 as Calgary’s first mayor, he died in 1910.

One of a Scots-Australian dynasty of bearers of the Murdoch name who include the media tycoon Rupert Murdoch, Professor Walter Murdoch was born in 1874.

The youngest of fourteen children of the Church of Scotland minister the Rev James Murdoch and his wife Helen, he was aged 10 when the family emigrated from Scotland to settle in Melbourne, Australia.

Becoming a leading academic and man of letters and renowned not only for his intelligence but also for his humanity, he was a chancellor and founding professor of English at the University of Western Australia, Perth, while Murdoch University, also in Perth, is named in his honour.

Also honoured with a knighthood, he died in 1970, and one of his nephews was the Australian journalist and media mogul Sir Keith Murdoch, who syndicated many of his uncle’s essays through his newspaper network.

Born in Melbourne in 1885, his parents, the Rev Patrick Murdoch and his wife Annie, had emigrated from Scotland to Australia three years earlier.

Foregoing the opportunity of a university education in favour of a career in the press, the Melbourne newspaper The Age employed him as district correspondent for the Malvern area.

But his early career as a pressman was hampered by a stammer and shyness brought about by this impediment.

He moved to London in 1908 to undergo speech therapy, eventually and through the influence of family friends who included no less a figure than the then Australian Prime Minister Alfred Deakin, gaining employment with the London-based Pall Mall magazine.

Although a talented journalist, his stammer and shyness continued to prove impediments to his work and the magazine, reluctantly, dismissed him.

Undaunted, he returned to Australia and The Age, working for a time as its Parliamentary reporter and forging valuable relationships with figures who included the future Australian Prime Minister Andrew Fisher.

He was despatched during the First World War as a correspondent to Gallipoli, in Turkey, where Australian and New Zealand troops were among those engaged in what proved to be the senseless carnage of the Dardanelles Campaign.

He used his political connections to circumvent strict censorship and furnish the Australian government and the British Cabinet with a damning report on the conduct of the campaign.

The chilling report was also later published in British newspapers and led to Sir Ian Hamilton, commander of the Dardanelles Campaign, being relieved of command.

By 1921, Murdoch had become chief editor of the Melbourne Herald and he later acquired the Sydney Sun – destined to become Australia’s biggest-selling newspaper.

Other media acquisitions followed, including radio stations, and in 1935 he formed Australian Associated Press Ltd.

Knighted in 1933, he died in 1952 and, while much of his estate had to be sold off to pay death duties, the Murdoch family was still left in full control of News Limited, proprietors of the Adelaide News.

His widow is Dame Elizabeth Murdoch, whom he married in 1928.

A noted philanthropist, she was born in Melbourne in 1909, her paternal grandfather having been William Greene, a Scottish railway engineer who had immigrated to Australia.

Appointed a Dame Commander of the British Empire in 1963, she is also the recipient of an honorary doctorate of laws from the University of Melbourne in recognition of her contribution to research, the arts and philanthropy.

She and her late husband had four children, one of whom is Keith Rupert Murdoch, better known as the international media tycoon Rupert Murdoch.

Born in Melbourne in 1931, and beginning with control of the Adelaide News following his father’s death, he has risen to become chairman and chief executive of News Corporation – a global media empire that includes ownership of newspapers, radio stations and cable television networks.

Ranked in 2010 by the prestigious Forbes magazine as the 13th most powerful person in the world and also listed as the 117th wealthiest person in the world, he has also, sometimes controversially, enjoyed personal audiences with politicians who include former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and American President Barack Obama.

Buying what was then the British broadsheet newspaper the Sun in 1969 and transforming it into a hugely successful tabloid, he created BskyB in 1990 by merging his satellite network Sky Television with British Satellite Broadcasting.

In 2006 his media empire itself became the centre of a storm of controversy over allegations that some of its titles, particularly the News of the World, the top-selling Sunday ‘sister’ title of the Sun, hacked mobile telephones to obtain titbits of information on celebrities, royalty and public citizens.

This culminated five years later, in July of 2011, when it was revealed that a private investigator had been hired by the News of the World to intercept the voice mail of the missing British teenager Milly Dowler, who was later found murdered.

With widespread public disgust over the revelations, News International announced the closure of the newspaper, while Murdoch resigned as its director.

It was as a condition of rules that disbar non-American citizens from owning U.S. television stations that he took up American citizenship, allowing him to set up the Fox Broadcasting Company – but as a consequence losing his Australian citizenship.

Married four times, it was through his marriage from 1967 to 1999 to his second wife, the Scots-born journalist Anna Torv, that he is the father of Elisabeth, James and Lachlan Murdoch.

Born in 1968 in Sydney, his daughter Elisabeth is the business executive who set up the British-based Shine Limited television production company in 2001.

His son James, born in 1972, holds posts that include chairman and chief executive of News Corporation for Europe and Asia, while Lachlan Murdoch, born in 1971, is a former News Corporation executive.

history_legacy:
Clan Napier are a Lowland clan. Traditionally said to descend from the ancient Earls of Lennox, the name Napier is rumoured to come from the word "naperer" - meaning a person who was in charge of table linens within a household.

In the 15th century Alexander Napier because the 1st Lord of Merchiston, and was made Provost of Edinburgh after making his fortune as a merchant in the city. The clan's influence can be widely seen in Edinburgh - Napier University has a Merchison campus, the grounds of which contain the former clan seat Merchiston Tower.

The Napier clan motto is "Sans tache" (Without stain) and the clan crest is an arm with a crescent in hand.

name: O'Brien
history_irish:
Of high degree

Of truly ancient and illustrious pedigree, the O’Briens of today can boast a descent from the famed Race of Cas, also known as the DalgCais, or Dalcassians.

The Dalcassians were named from the legendary Cormac Cas, the early to mid-third century chieftain of the province of Munster who was renowned for his remarkable courage, strength, and dexterity.

This progenitor of the O’Briens inflicted a celebrated defeat on the men of the province of Leinster in a battle fought near present day Wexford, but was killed in battle in 254A.D. at Dun-tri-Liag, or the Fort of the Stone Slabs, known today as Duntrileague, in Co. Limerick.

His deathblow, according to the ancient annals, came from the spear of the Leinster king known rather colourfully as Eochy of the Red Eyebrows.

But it is from a descendant of Cormac Cas that the O’Briens take their name.

This is no less a figure than Brian Bóruma mac Cénnetig, a younger son of Cénnetig, king of Thomond, in the northern reaches of the province of Munster, and who was born about 926A.D.

Late tenth and early eleventh century Ireland was the scene of vicious inter-clan rivalry as successive clan chiefs fought for supremacy over their rivals, and it was this disunity that worked to the advantage of Viking invaders.

The period 795A.D. to 1014A.D. is known to Irish history as The Viking Tyranny, and it was largely through the inspired leadership of Brian Boru that Viking power was diminished, although not completely eliminated.

He was able to achieve this by managing to rally a number of other chieftains to his cause – although by no means all.

With his battle-hardened warriors known as the Dalcassian knights at his side, Boru had by 1002A.D. achieved the prize of the High Kingship of Ireland – but there were still rival chieftains, and not least the Vikings, to deal with.

These Vikings, known as Ostmen, had occupied and fortified Dublin in the mid-ninth century and had other important trading settlements in other parts of the island.

Resenting Boru’s High Kingship, a number of chieftains, particularly those of the province of Leinster, found common cause with the Ostmen, and the two sides met in final and bloody confrontation at the battle of Clontarf, four miles north of Dublin, on Good Friday 1014.

Boru proved victorious, but the annals speak of great slaughter on the day, with the dead piled high on the field of battle.

Among the many dead were Brian Boru’s three sons, while he was killed by a party of fleeing Vikings, but not before felling most of them with his great two-handed sword.

His descendants rapidly consolidated their power base in Thomond, ruling there for centuries as kings and princes of Thomond and amassing other honours and titles along the way.

Meanwhile other branches of the clan spread into areas that include the north of the present day Co. Tipperary, Co. Clare, and in present day Co. Limerick, where they gave their name to what is now the barony of Pubbelebrien.

Titles acquired by the O’Briens over the centuries include Barons and Earls of Inchiquin, Viscounts of Clare, and Earls and Marquises of Thomond.

At the time of writing Conor Myles O’Brien, born in Surrey, England, in 1943, is the proud holder of the titles of The O’Brien, Prince of Thomond, the 18th Baron Inchiquin, and 10th Baronet of Leamaneh.

Recognised as Chief of the Name of the O’Briens, he now lives on Drumoland Estate in Thomond House, next to Drumoland Castle, Co. Clare, which was the seat of the O’Briens until the early 1960s.

Turning back the pages of history, Brian Boru’s younger son, Tiege, was killed by his brother Donagh who, after a reign of nearly 50 years as King of Munster, and for reasons presumably best known to himself, became a monk after travelling on pilgrimage to Rome.

It was one of his descendants, Donagh Cairbre, who lived from 1194 until 1242, who was the first to adopt the Ó Briain, or O’Brien, surname – indicating descent from Brian Boru and with the name also held to indicate ‘exalted’, ‘eminence’, or ‘of great strength.’

Great strength was certainly needed on the part of the O’Briens to retain their ancient heritage, particularly in the wake of the early twelfth century Cambro-Norman invasion of the Emerald Isle and subsequent consolidation of power of the English Crown.

England’s Henry II landed in Ireland in October of 1171 with the aim of curbing the power of his Norman barons who had invaded the faction-riven island in 1169 and swiftly amassed territory.

But protracted war between the king and his barons was averted when they submitted to the royal will, promising homage and allegiance in return for holding the territories they had conquered in the king’s name.

Henry also received the reluctant submission and homage of many of the Irish chieftains, tired as they were with internecine warfare and also perhaps realising that as long as they were rivals and not united they were no match for the powerful forces the English Crown could muster.

Among their number was Donal Cairbre, father of the Donagh Cairbre who was the first to take the surname of O’Brien.

English dominion over Ireland was ratified through the Treaty of Windsor of 1175, under the terms of which Donal Cairbre and other native Irish chieftains were only allowed to rule territory unoccupied by the Normans in the role of a vassal of the king.

It only proved to be a recipe for disaster as the island was frequently torn apart by bloody insurrection and rebellion against the increasingly harsh policies of the English Crown.

The treatment meted out to the native Irish is graphically and eloquently expressed in a desperate plea sent to Pope John XII by Roderick O’Carroll of Ely, Donald O’Neil of Ulster, and a number of other Irish chieftains in 1318.

They stated: ‘As it very constantly happens, whenever an Englishman, by perfidy or craft, kills an Irishman, however noble, or however innocent, be he clergy or layman, there is no penalty or correction enforced against the person who may be guilty of such wicked murder.

‘But rather the more eminent the person killed and the higher rank which he holds among his own people, so much more is the murderer honoured and rewarded by the English, and not merely by the people at large, but also by the religious and bishops of the English race.’

Tragically the O’Briens, in common with other native Irish families, often found themselves on opposing sides in the rebellions that broke out in increasingly explosive and bloody fury.

Fire and sword

A parliament was hastily summoned in Ireland in 1536 by England’s Henry VIII to rubber stamp the policy of religious reformation that he had already established in England - effectively disestablishing the Roman Catholic faith and confiscating Irish monastic property to the English Crown.

Among those who complied with the monarch’s demands to the parliament was Murrough O’Brien, 1st Earl of Thomond, obviously too well aware of the consequences in terms of lands and titles should he have refused.

This policy of accommodation with the English Crown on the part of some O’Briens continued under Donogh O’Brien, 4th Earl of Thomond, during the rebellion from 1594 to 1603 known as the Nine Years War.

The rebel leaders received aid from Spain in the form of a Spanish invasion force that landed at Kinsale in 1601 under the command of Don Juan del Águila.

Joined by a rebel army from Ulster, in the north, it was defeated following the siege of Kinsale, however, and Águila surrendered to Lord Mountjoy, Queen Elizabeth’s Lord Deputy for Ireland.

The Earl of Thomond had commanded 1,000 men, and the bravery he had displayed was held to have been a significant factor in the eventual defeat of the rebels.

His reward came in 1605 when he was appointed President of Munster and Commander-in-Chief of of the English forces in the province.

More than 35 years later Murrough O’Brien, the 6th Baron of Inchiquin, earned himself the notorious title of Murrough of the Burnings, brutally ravaging rebel strongholds, including Cashel, with fire and sword.

This was during the insurrection that devastated the island between 1641 and 1652.

At the root of the rebellion was the Crown’s policy of settling, or ‘planting’ loyal Protestants on Irish land, a policy that had started during the reign of Henry VIII.

In the insurrection that erupted in 1641, at least 2,000 Protestant settlers were massacred, while thousands more were stripped of their belongings and driven from their lands to seek refuge where they could.

Their revenge came nine years later in the sinister form of Oliver Cromwell, who had become self-styled Lord Protector of England following the execution of Charles I.

He descended on Ireland at the head of a 20,000-strong army of Parliamentary troops in August of 1649 and, with the aid of allies such as Murrough of the Burnings, soon suppressed the rebellion and held the island in a grip of iron.

One of the island’s many Cromwellian victims was Terence O’Brien, the Roman Catholic bishop of Emly who had been born in Limerick, at the head of the estuary of the river Shannon, in 1600.

Siding with the rebels and treating their wounded, he helped to organise the resistance when the Parliamentary forces invaded Limerick in October of 1651.

But resistance ultimately proved futile and the city was forced to surrender.

Denied quarter and protection, the bishop, along with a Father Wolf and a Major General Purcell, were brought before a court martial and hanged.

The bishop and sixteen other Irish Catholic martyrs were officially blessed centuries later by Pope John Paul II.

Cromwell’s aim had been to quash all forms of rebellion, to ‘remove’ all Catholic landowners who had taken part in the insurrection, and to convert the native Irish to the Protestant faith.

Towards this end Catholic landowners who had taken part in the rebellion had their estates confiscated.

Among those who suffered from this policy was Daniel O’Brien, Viscount Clare, who had been a member of the rebel controlling body known as the Supreme Council of Catholic Confederates.

The 3rd Viscount Clare, also named Daniel O’Brien, who died in 1690, was forced to seek a new life abroad in the years following the Cromwellian conquest of his native land and was responsible for raising the famed regiment of the Irish Brigade known as Clare’s Dragoons.

The regiment fought in the service of Britain’s enemy, France, and its exploits are recalled in the first verse of the song Clare’s Dragoons, concerning the battle of Ramilles in 1706 in which Charles O’Brien, the 5th Viscount Clare, was killed:

When on Ramilles’ bloody field

The baffled French were forced to yield,

The victor Saxon backward reeled

Before the charge of Clare’s Dragoons.

His son, also Charles O’Brien, the 6th Viscount Clare, who was born in 1699 and died in 1771, also fought in French service, becoming a Marshall of France.

An Act of Union between Great Britain and Ireland was passed in 1800, and this served to fuel the flames of further rebellion.

There was a short-lived and abortive rebellion in the summer of 1848 by a movement known as the Young Irelanders, who sought repeal of the union, and one of its leading lights was William Smith O’Brien, born in Dromoland Castle, Co. Clare, in 1803 and who died in 1864.

Young Irelanders such as O’Brien had advocated the non-payment of rents and the tearing up of railway lines in a desperate bid to stop the removal of vital food supplies from the island during the terrible time from 1845 to 1849 known as the Great Hunger, caused by the failure of the potato crop.

His daughter Charlotte Grace O’Brien and his brother Edward O’Brien were also committed to the cause of Home Rule, as was the author and Roman Catholic priest Richard O’Brien, born in 1809 in Carrick-on-Suir, Co. Tipperary.

A founder in 1849 of the Catholic Young Men’s Society, he was also a regular contributor to the Irish Catholic magazine The Irish Monthly, and The Nation.

Another leading campaigner for independence from Britain was the revolutionary James Francis Xavier O’Brien, born in 1828 in Dungarvan, Co. Waterford, but better known as J.F.X. O’Brien.

At the age of 21 he took part in an attack on a police barracks but managed to escape arrest.

Studying medicine at both Queens College, in Galway, and in Paris, he returned to Ireland for a brief time before setting sail in 1856 for New Orleans, later becoming an assistant surgeon for a time in the Union Army during the American Civil War.

O’Brien had joined the Fenian Brotherhood, a secret society dedicated to achieving Ireland’s independence through revolutionary means, while in America.

On his return to his native land in 1862 he joined the Irish Republican Brotherhood (I.R.B.) and played a role in the abortive Fenian Rising of 1867.

Taking part in an I.R.B. attack on the Ballyknockan police barracks, he was arrested, tried for high treason, and sentenced to death – but this was commuted to imprison-ment.

Following his release after an amnesty in 1869 he became president of the Supreme Council of the Irish Republican Brotherhood, but left the organisation about four years later.

O’Brien later served as a Member of Parliament for South Mayo from 1885 to 1895 and for Cork City from 1895 to 1905, in addition to serving from 1900 until his death in 1905 as general secretary of the United Irish League of Great Britain.

name: O'Rourke
history_irish:
Warrior kings

A clan with a truly royal pedigree, the O’Rourkes were from earliest times settled in Connacht – which, along with Ulster, Munster, and Leinster is one of the four ancient provinces of the Emerald Isle.

The Gaelic-Irish form of the name is ‘Ó Ruairc’, derived from the Old Norse ‘Hrothreker’, denoting ‘famous king’ – an apt description considering that the O’Rourkes held the kingship of Connacht throughout both the tenth and eleventh centuries.

But their royal lineage goes back much further, indicated by the fact that they were members, along with the O’Connors, Malones, Flanagans, MacDermots and others, of the tribal grouping known as the Uí Briuin.

All these clans trace a proud descent from Niall Noíghiallach, better known to posterity as the great warrior king Niall of the Nine Hostages, through his brother Briuin, or Brian.

The dramatic life and times of Niall are steeped in stirring Celtic myth and legend.

The youngest son of Eochaidh Mugmedon, king of Connacht, his mother died in childbirth and he was brought up by his evil stepmother Mongfhinn who, for reasons best known to herself, was determined that he should die.

She accordingly abandoned him naked on the Hill of Tara, inauguration site of the Ard Rí, or High Kings, of Ireland, but he was found by a wandering bard who took him back to his father.

One legend is that Mongfhinn sent Niall and his four brothers – Brian, Fiachra, Ailill, and Fergus – to a renowned prophet who was also a blacksmith to determine which of them would succeed their father as Ard Rí.

The blacksmith, known as Sitchin, set the lads a task by deliberately setting fire to his forge.

Niall’s brothers ran in and came out carrying the spearheads, fuel, hammers, and barrels of beer they had rescued, but Niall staggered out clutching the heavy anvil so vital to the blacksmith’s trade.

By this deed, Sitchin prophesied that Niall would be the one who would take on the glorious mantle of kingship.

Another prophetic incident occurred one day while Niall and his brothers were engaged in the hunt.

Thirsty from their efforts they encountered an ugly old woman who offered them water – but only in return for a kiss.

Three of the lads, no doubt repelled by her green teeth and scaly skin, refused. Fiachra pecked her lightly on the cheek and, by this act, she prophesied that he would one day reign at Tara – but only briefly.

The bold Niall, however, kissed her fully on the lips. The hag then demanded that he should now have full sexual intercourse with her and, undaunted, he did so.

Through this action she was suddenly transformed into a stunningly beautiful young woman known as Flaithius, or Royalty, who predicted that he would become the greatest High King of Ireland.

His stepmother Mongfhinn later tried to poison him, but accidentally took the deadly potion herself and died.

This legend relates to what was known as the Festival of Mongfhinn, or Feis na Samhan (the Feast of Samhain), because it was on the evening of October 31, on Samhain’s Eve, that the poisoning incident is said to have taken place.

It was believed for centuries in Ireland that, on Samhain Eve, Mongfhinn’s warped and wicked spirit would roam the land in hungry search of children’s souls.

The Festival, or Feast, of Samhain, is today better known as Halloween.

Niall became Ard Rí in 379 A.D. and embarked on the series of military campaigns and other daring adventures that would subsequently earn him the title of Niall of the Nine Hostages.

The nine countries and territories into which he raided and took hostages for ransom were all four Irish provinces, Britain, and the territories of the Saxons, Morini, Picts, and Dalriads.

Niall’s most famous hostage was a young lad known as Succat, son of Calpernius, a Romano-Briton who lived in the area of present day Milford Haven, on the Welsh coast.

Later known as Patricius, or Patrick, he became renowned as Ireland’s patron saint, St. Patrick, responsible for bringing the light of Christianity to the island in the early years of the fifth century A.D.

Raiding in Gaul, in the area of Boulogne-sur-mer in present day France, Niall was ambushed and killed by one of his treacherous subjects in 405 A.D.

But his legacy survived through the royal dynasties and clans founded by his sons and brothers such as Brian.

West Bréifne, now modern day Co. Leitrim, was the O’Rourke territory, and accordingly was known as Bréifne O’Rourke, while East Bréifne, now Co. Cavan, was held by their neighbours the O’Reillys and was known as Bréifne O’Reilly.

The present day town of Manorhamilton, in the north of Leitrim, was known formerly as O’Rourke’s Little Field, but their stronghold was Drom Ath Thiar, or Dromahaire - signifying ‘The Ridge of the Western Ford.’

Built by Fhergal O’Rourke in the mid-tenth century, the imposing Dromahaire Castle was situated near the River Bonet, while their banqueting hall stood nearby.

The O’Rourkes were famed for their lavish hospitality, and it was in this banqueting hall that they hosted their legendary feasts.

These feasts were so renowned that they became the subject of numerous poems and songs, and the satirist Jonathan Swift, born in Dublin in 1667, penned his own ode to the O’Rourkes in a series of verses that begin:

O’Rourke’s noble fare

Will ne’er be forgot

By those who were there,

And those who were not.

His revels to keep,

We sup and we dine,

On seven score sheep,

Fat bullocks and swine.

By the turn of the twelfth century the O’Rourkes, in common with other Connacht clans, had come under the overlordship of the Royal House of O’Connor, which, in addition to its kingship of the province, also furnished some of the island’s celebrated Ard Rí.

This close kinship with the O’Connors was to place them at the very heart of the momentous events that shook the island in the late twelfth century when it was invaded by ambitious and battle-hardened Norman barons from Wales.

A power struggle had existed between Rory O’Connor, king of Connacht, and Dermot MacMurrough, king of Leinster.

It was as part of this struggle that MacMurrough, allied with Muirchertach MacLochlainn, king of the powerful O’Neills, enlisted the aid of the barons in 1169.

Although the consequences could not have been foreseen at the time, this led to the eventual consolidation of the power of the English Crown over the island.

The O’Rourkes had been involved in dealings with Dermot MacMurrough some years before the invasion when Devorgilla, wife of the O’Rourke chieftain Tiernan O’Rourke, had run off with the Leinster king.

The passionate affair burned itself out after two years, and MacMurrough was eventually forced to pay O’Rourke 100 ounces of gold as ‘compensation.’

A chastened Devorgilla, meanwhile, took herself back to her father and dedicated the rest of her life to the building of a fine church at Clonmacnoise.

But infinitely more serious than Devorgilla’s infidelity were the consequences of the Norman invasion that had been partly instigated by her erstwhile lover.

Land-hungry barons and their followers, with the active encouragement of the English Crown, wrested territory from the native Irish such as the O’Rourkes and the island became a battleground.

One of the many early victims was an O’Rourke chieftain, also known as Tiernan, who had his head cut from his shoulders by a sword wielded by the haughty and powerful Norman baron Hugh de Lacy.

The head was then taken to Dublin, which had become the bastion of the Crown in Ireland, and triumphantly impaled on one of the city gates as a macabre warning to others.

But the O’Rourkes and other native Irish clans did not simply bow down and meekly accept their fate.

Battle-axe and broadsword

Known in his native tongue as Brian na Múrtha Ó Ruairc, Brian O’Rourke became one of the many heroes of the resistance to English dominance of Ireland.

Born in about 1540, he took over the leadership of his clan when he was aged in his ‘twenties – and one indication of his ruthlessness is that he achieved this by murdering his older brothers.

He had been knighted by the English in a bid to secure his allegiance – this at a time when Connacht was ruled in the form of the English-imposed Presidency of Connacht – but he proved a difficult character to handle.

Sir Henry Sidney, Lord Deputy of Ireland, described him as the proudest man he had ever dealt with, while another contemporary described him as ‘the proudest man this day living on the earth.’

By 1585 he was being described by the English powers as being ‘somewhat learned, but of an insolent and proud nature and no further obedient than is constrained by Her Majesty’s forces.’

O’Rourke finally revealed where his true allegiance lay through his involvement in the rescue of shipwrecked survivors of the Spanish Armada in September of 1588.

The 130-strong Spanish fleet, intent on the invasion of England, had been scattered in heavy storms after its defeat at the battle of Gravelines, and many vessels driven towards the west coast of Ireland.

This caused alarm on the part of the English authorities on the island, who feared, not without justification, that the disaffected native Irish would rally to their rescue.

William Fitzwilliam, then Lord Deputy of Ireland, even sanctioned the use of torture against survivors, while also ordering that anyone who came to their aid would be declared traitors.

At least 24 Spanish vessels are believed to have been wrecked on the coastline – from Co. Antrim in the north to Co. Kerry in the south.

One of the ships was La Trinidad Valencera, which had already taken on survivors of the shipwrecked Barca de Amburgo.

Grossly overladen and listing in heavy seas, the order was given to abandon ship as she lay in Glenagivney Bay, in Co. Donegal.

Up to 560 soaked and exhausted survivors managed to make their way ashore, but were intercepted by a heavily armed body of troops.

Trusting to the mercy of the authorities, they had no sooner surrendered their arms than the officers and noblemen were separated from the group and 300 of the ordinary seamen massacred on the spot.

It was learned by the English that Brian O’Rourke, despite the grave risk to himself and his family, had rescued eighty Spanish sailors who had been washed up on a different part of the coast and managed to get them safely off the island.

This sealed his fate as, by the spring of 1590, government forces occupied his territory and he was forced to flee.

By February of 1591, the government of England’s Elizabeth I learned he was in Scotland, seeking the aid of the Scots monarch James VI who, twelve years later, became James I of England and Ireland.

With his eye no doubt on his succession to the throne following Elizabeth’s death, James refused to even grant O’Rourke an audience and agreed to his arrest and delivery into English custody.

Arrested in Glasgow in April of 1591, he was duly taken into custody and hauled off to grim imprisonment in the Tower of London – but not before an outraged mob of Glaswegians had rioted in a bid to prevent his extradition to England.

Despite their king’s understandable pragmatic stance on the matter, it would appear that the Scots still retained a close bond of kinship with their Celtic cousins from across the North Channel.

Tried for treason in a mockery of a trial in October of 1591, the proud and defiant Brian O’Rourke was found guilty and hanged, drawn and quartered on the bloody execution ground of Tyburn only a few days later.

But rather than acting as a dire warning to his O’Rourke kinsfolk, his execution only served to fuel the flames of further rebellion in Ireland – notably in the form of Cogadh na Naoi mBliama, or the Nine Years War.

One of the leading rebel commanders in this war was one of Brian O’Rourke’s sons, the gloriously named Brian Oge na Samhthach Ó Ruairc – better known as Young Brian of the Axes.

Armed with battle-axe and broadsword, he and his O’Rourke followers allied themselves with the forces of Hugh O’Neill, Earl of Tyrone, and those of Red Hugh O’Donnell and others that included the famed and feared cavalry of the Gallaghers.

They literally set the island ablaze in a vicious campaign of guerrilla warfare, wreaking a whirlwind of devastation on English settlements and garrisons in a daring series of lightning raids.

A defeat was inflicted on an English army at the battle of Clontibert, while in August of 1598 another significant defeat was inflicted at the battle of Yellow Ford.

But the most significant defeat inflicted on the English forces during the Nine Years War came at the battle of Curlew Pass, fought on the hot summer day of August 15th, 1599, near Boyle, Co. Roscommon, in the northwest of the island.

With Young Brian of the Axes among their ranks, the rebels ambushed an English force under the command of Sir Conyers Clifford at a pass through the imposing Curlew Mountains and routed them.

The English lost at least 500 men, including Sir Conyers Clifford, whose head was cut off and triumphantly given to Red Hugh O’Donnell.

The Curlew Pass was the scene of another rebel victory later in the war, while the battlefield today is overlooked by a magnificent sculpture,‘The Gaelic Chieftain’, which was executed by the sculptor Maurice Harron and placed there in 1999.

Overlooking the Curlew Pass, it can be seen while driving along the route known as National 4.

Meanwhile, as English control over Ireland teetered on the brink of collapse, thousands of troops were hastily despatched to the island and, in the face of the over-whelming odds against them, Red Hugh and the Earl of Tyrone sought help from Spain, England’s enemy.

A well-equipped Spanish army under General del Aquila landed at Kinsale in December of 1601, but was forced into surrender only a few weeks later, in January of 1602.

Resistance continued until 1603, but proved abortive, and Young Brian of the Axes was forced into hiding – eventually finding refuge far from his own territory at Rosserilly Monastery, in Co. Galway.

It was here that he died, while what remained of his followers eked out a precarious existence in the more inhospitable parts of West Bréifne, while the territory was strongly garrisoned by English troops.

The O’Rourkes never recovered from the blow and many were forced to seek a new life on foreign shores.

Others left the island in the wake of the devastating Cromwellian invasion of 1649 – an invasion that followed a rebellion that broke out on the island in 1641.

Still more O’Rourkes and other Gaelic-Irish fled the island following the abortive war from 1688 to 1691 in support of the deposed Stuart monarch James II.

One noted exile was Father Manus O’Rourke who, from his new homeland of France, compiled great works wistfully written in the Irish language.

Others found refuge in Poland and Russia and later formed part of the aristocracy of these nations – including Joseph O’Rourke, who became Prince Joseph O’Rourke, a high-ranking general in the army of the Russian Empire.
