James VI, who was certainly no friend of his unruly subjects in the far-flung Highlands and Islands, resolved to make an example of the troublesome MacGregors once and for all, describing them as ‘the wicked and unhappy race of the Clan Gregor’, and determining to ‘pursue and prosecute them with all rigour and extremity’.

Matters came to a bloody head for the MacGregors in February of 1603 when they met their deadly foes, the Colquhouns of Luss, in battle at Glenfruin, near Loch Lomond.

Subsequent accounts of the MacGregors’ actions on the day were grossly exaggerated, but they did indeed kill at least sixty Colquhouns, including the Laird of Luss, before ravaging their lands and making off with a rich booty of cattle, sheep, goats and horses.

An incensed James VI arranged for the passing of an Act of Council that imposed severe sanctions on the clan.

These measures included the proscription, or banning, of the very name MacGregor itself.

MacGregor of Glenstrae, the Clan Chief, was hanged along with eleven of his leading men at the Mercat Cross in Edinburgh, while a price of £1000 was put on the heads of other prominent members of the clan.

A lower sum was put on the heads of other MacGregors, and any clansman who brought in the head of one of his kinsmen was to be granted a full pardon – an option that very few, if any, MacGregor clansmen chose to exercise.

It was not until 1774 that the proscription on the name MacGregor was at last lifted and, while many who had been forced to adopt new names reverted back to MacGregor, others who had chosen aliases such as Orr retained this new name.

Politics and law

Not only in their original homelands but also in other lands, bearers of the Orr name have exerted a significant influence.

While not quite on the battlefield himself, the Scots-born Hugh Orr played a significant role in America’s War of Independence from 1775 to 1783 against its colonial master Britain.

Born in the village of Lochwinnoch, Renfrewshire, he immigrated to America in 1737 at the age of 20 after having been apprenticed as a metal worker.

Siding with the cause of his newly adopted homeland against colonial rule, he manufactured guns and ammunition for the Colonial Army.

But, in addition to forging weapons of destruction, he also pioneered the manufacture of edged tools for making agricultural implements and other commodities useful to the peaceful growth of the young nation; he died in 1798.

Back across the Atlantic to Britain and late nineteenth century politics, Sir Archibald Orr-Ewing was the son of the wealthy Glasgow merchant William Ewing, while his mother was a daughter of John Orr, Provost of Paisley.

Born in 1847, he served as Conservative Member of Parliament (MP) for Dunbartonshire from 1868 to 1892 in addition to serving as Dean of Faculties at Glasgow University and Ensign-General of the Royal Company of Archers.

Raised to the Peerage of the United Kingdom in 1886 as 1st Baronet Orr-Ewing, of the Orr-Ewing Baronetcy of Ballikinrain, Stirlingshire, his imposing stately home of Ballikinrain is now a private residential school. He died in 1893.

His youngest son was the soldier and politician Charles Lindsay Orr-Ewing, who served for a time as a captain in the 3rd Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders.

From 1895 until his death in 1903, he served as Conservative MP for the former constituency of Ayr Burghs.

Another soldier and politician of the Orr name was Robert Orr, born in 1917 in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and who died in 2004.

Awarded the Legion of Merit after serving as a major with the U.S. quartermaster general staff during the Second World War, he later turned to politics.

Representing Evansville as a Republican from 1968 to 1973 in the Indiana Senate and, from 1981 to 1989 as 45th Governor of Indiana, he also served under President George H.W. Bush from 1989 to 1992 as U.S. Ambassador to Singapore.

While some Orrs who may originally have been MacGregors adopted the name to distance themselves from their lawless reputation, others of the name have been distinctly and notably on the side of the law.

Two in particular, by coincidence sharing both the same forename and honorific title, have served as Chief Constable of a Scottish police force.

Born in 1918, Sir John Orr became a clerk with the former City of Edinburgh Police after being educated at the city’s George Heriot’s School.

Rising rapidly through the ranks after becoming a police constable, he was appointed Chief Constable of the former Lothian and Peebles Police and, in 1975 following the merger of a number of forces, the first Chief Constable of Lothian and Borders Police.

A recipient of the Queen’s Police Medal and an OBE, he was also honoured in 1979 with a knighthood in recognition of his services to policing.

Also a talented rugby player in his younger days, having played for the Scottish Rugby Union (SRU) on two occasions, he served as its president from 1975 until 1976.

He died in 1995, while his equally distinguished namesake is Sir John Orr, who served as Chief Constable of Strathclyde Police from 1996 to 2001.

Born in 1945 and joining the former Renfrew and Bute Constabulary in 1961, he has also served as deputy, then Chief Constable, of Dumfries and Galloway Constabulary.

It was while he was a Detective Chief Superintendent and joint head of Strathclyde CID that he first became more widely known to the public at large as the senior investigating officer of the Lockerbie bombing in December of 1988.

This was when Pan Am Flight 103 from London to New York blew up in the skies above the Scottish town, killing 259 passengers and crew and eleven people on the ground.

The investigation headed by Orr, which led to the conviction and imprisonment of Libyan Abdelbaset-al-Megrahi, was the biggest single murder investigation in the history of Scottish policing.

Following his extensive investigation of the bombing, he lectured throughout the world on disaster planning, investigation and administration.

Recipient of a diploma in forensic medicine from Glasgow University and graduating from the FBI National Executive Institute Course in Virginia in 1997, he was honoured with a knighthood in 2001.

One particularly prominent and distinguished bearer of the Orr name and one whose pioneering work still benefits millions of people across the world to this day, was the Scottish doctor, biologist and nutritionist John Boyd Orr, 1st Baron Boyd-Orr.

Born in 1880 in the small East Ayrshire village of Kilmaurs, near Kilmarnock, he went on to become a leading campaigner for more equitable food distribution throughout the world and the recipient of a Nobel Peace Prize.

One of seven children, his father, Robert, was a quarry owner while his mother Annie, née Orr, was the daughter of a quarry owner.

Winning a bursary to Kilmarnock Academy when he was aged 13, he later became a pupil teacher in the village of West Kilbride, to where his family had moved, while also studying for teacher training and university entrance qualifications and working part-time for his father.

Entering teacher training college and also Glasgow University at the age of 19, he was shocked by the poverty and malnutrition of the children he taught as part of his training course – and these impressions would remain with him for the rest of his life.

Qualifying as a teacher and teaching for a time in the Ayrshire town of Saltcoats, he later returned to Glasgow University to study both biology and medicine.

Despite the rigours of the courses, he qualified in both subjects.

A brief period followed as a ship’s surgeon on a trading vessel plying its trade between Scotland and West Africa, before embarking on a two-year Carnegie Research Scholarship to study everything from malnutrition to how much energy military recruits expended in training.

In April of 1914, the future Nobel Prize winner took charge of a new research institute into animal nutrition in Aberdeen - later to become internationally famous as the Rowett Research Institute.

The outbreak of the First World War later that year interrupted his work with the institute, with Orr working with both the Royal Army Medical Corps and the Royal Navy on methods of improving the hygiene of recruitment training camps and the nutrition of soldiers in the trenches.

Returning to the Rowett Research Institute, Orr expanded its remit to include human nutrition, while he also campaigned for wide-ranging improvements in people’s diets.

Resigning from the institute at the end of the Second World War and becoming the first director general of the United Nations Food and Agricultural Organisation (FAO), he put forward plans for improving food distribution and for its more equitable distribution throughout the world.

Recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize in 1949 for his work with the FAO and research into nutrition, he donated the financial portion of the prize to ‘world peace and a unified world government’.

Elevated to the Peerage of the United Kingdom in 1949 as Baron Boyd-Orr, he was elected eleven years later as first president of the World Academy of Art and Science – set up by scientists concerned about potential misuse of scientific discoveries, particularly nuclear weapons.

He died in 1971, and is honoured through two buildings named after him at Glasgow University, including the Boyd Orr Centre for Population and Ecosystem Health, while his Nobel Medal is held in the university’s Hunterian Museum.

name: Milne
history_scottish:
Flames of martyrdom

The most common form in Scotland of the mainly English ‘Mill’ or ‘Mills’, ‘Milne’ is also more or less interchangeable with ‘Mylne’, found mainly in the northeast.

With the Milne and Mylne forms believed to be of peculiarly Scottish genesis, the name has two possible sources of origin.

The commonly accepted derivation is from the English ‘mylen’, indicating a miller or someone who lived near a corn mill.

But a closer examination of the historical record reveals a rather more intriguing source – one that stretches back through the mists of time to those battle-hardened knights who first arrived on English shores with the Norman Conquest of 1066, and the subsequent subjugation of the Anglo-Saxons.

In the Battle Abbey Roll – the list of those who fought at the side of William the Conqueror at the battle of Hastings – is a Guillaume de Moulins, or de Molyneux, from Moulineaux, near Rouen.

He was granted lands at Sefton, in Lancashire, and a later son of the family, Vivian de Molyneux, moved in the late twelfth century over the Border to Oxton, in Berwickshire, with further lands being acquired later at Saltoun, in East Lothian.

The move north had been at the invitation of the Scottish monarch David I, who had spent much of his early life at the court of England’s Henry I and become enamoured with Anglo-Norman customs and manners.

It was when he acceded to the throne of Scotland in 1124 that he welcomed Anglo-Normans such as Vivian de Moylneux into his country, granting them lands.

Evidence that they did indeed become established in the new Scottish territories, is that the signature of Elizabeth de Molyn, of Berwickshire, appears on the infamous Ragman Roll of 1296.

It had been in order to reinforce his domination of Scotland that England’s Edward I, known as the Hammer of the Scots, required Scots earls, bishops, burgesses and other landowners to sign a humiliating treaty of fealty to him.

This became known as the Ragman Roll because of the number of ribbons that dangled from the seals of the reluctant signatories.

The form ‘de Molyn’ illustrated by Elizabeth de Molyn’s name is believed by some experts to represent the gradual shift in Scotland from ‘de Molyneux’ to ‘Milne’, or ‘Mylne’ through a number of other forms such as ‘Molyn’.

Further evidence for the link between the Milnes and the original de Molyneux family is found in the fact that their respective Coats of Arms are almost identical, apart from the tinctures, or colours.

The Milne Coat of Arms features a blue cross against a gold background, while that of the de Molyneux Earls of Sefton show a gold cross against a blue background.

The Milnes and their namesakes the Mylnes have also for centuries been considered a sept of Clan Gordon, and the explanation for this goes back to the settlement in the Berwickshire area at the same time as the de Molyneux family of the Gordons.

An originally Anglo-Norman family, they are believed to have adopted the name ‘Gordon’ from ‘gor-dun’, indicating the ‘great hill fort’ near which they settled.

The township of Gordon grew up beside this ancient hill fort – not far from the Milne landholdings at Oxton and Saltoun.

The name of Milne and its other Scottish variations such as Mylne is recorded in Aberdeenshire in 1380.

It is believed the Berwickshire Milnes first moved there in the company of the more powerful Gordons, under whose protection they lived, in the early years of the fourteenth century when Sir Adam Gordon was granted the rich lands of Strathbogie.

As a sept of Clan Gordon, whose motto is ‘Abide’ and whose crest, in common with that of Milne, is a stag’s head, the Milnes subsequently shared in both the clan’s glorious fortunes and tragic misfortunes.

But, although much of the history of the Milnes is enmeshed with that of the Gordons, they nevertheless retained their own proud identity, illustrated by their personal motto of ‘As much by art as strength.’

One significant early battle in which the Milnes were bloodied while fighting in the ranks of Clan Gordon was the disastrous battle of Halidon Hill.

The great warrior king Robert the Bruce had died in 1329 and was succeeded by the five-year-old David II.

Eager to take advantage of a dispute among the Scottish nobles over the young king’s succession, an ambitious Edward III of England gave his support to the young king’s rival, Edward Balliol, confident he could use him as a mere puppet for his own imperialist aims.

A mighty English force invaded Scotland in August of 1332, defeating the Scots in battle at Dupplin Moor, near Perth; Balliol was enthroned as King of Scots at Scone the following month and, as Edward had plotted, swore fealty to him.

Nationalist passions were aroused, however, and Andrew Murray, who had been appointed Guardian of Scotland, raised the banner of revolt against the puppet Scots king and sent him fleeing across the border to his English master.

But in May of 1333 Edward returned with another army, laid siege to Berwick Castle, and met the Scots in battle at Halidon Hill, to the northwest of Berwick, on July 19.

Murray had already been captured and the new Guardian was Archibald, Lord of Douglas, who arranged his forces in three tightly packed groups of spearmen known as schiltrons, and a division of 1,200 knights that included the Gordon Chief, Sir Adam Gordon.

They proved no match, however, for the deadly skill of the English archers and the knights who had taken better strategic advantage of the terrain.

The English victory was so complete that while Douglas, Sir Adam Gordon, the earls of Ross, Sutherland, and Carrick, 500 knights, seventy barons, and thousands of Scots foot soldiers were slain, the English were reported to have lost only fourteen men.

In later centuries, the Gordons and their Milne kinsfolk were staunch supports of the exiled Royal House of Stuart, fighting with distinction during the abortive Risings of 1715 and 1745.

One Milne tradition concerns Alexander Milne, the particularly enthusiastic Jacobite – as supporters of the Stuarts were known - who was born in 1699.

During the ’45 Rising, a party of Government troops had forcibly quartered themselves on Milne’s property at Mill of Alvan, in Banffshire.

His protest took the dangerous form of loudly singing Jacobite songs, and it took the firm persuasion of his wife and daughters before he agreed to be quiet.

Milnes were also in the vanguard of religious protest, most notably Walter Milne, recognised as the last Protestant martyr to be executed in Scotland before the Reformation.

A former Roman Catholic priest from Lunan, near Aberdeen, he was burned at the stake for heresy in St Andrews in April 1558 on the orders of the Roman Catholic Archbishop John Hamilton.

His defiant retort after hearing sentence of death became inspirational for succeeding generations of Protestants:

‘I will not recant the truth. ‘I am corn, not chaff; I will not be blown away by the wind or burst by the flail. I will survive both.’

His martyrdom is commemorated by the Martyrs’ Monument in St Andrews.

It was in the creative field of architecture that Milnes, with the spelling variant of Mylne, achieved fame and distinction that endures to this day.

This was through the family of the Mylnes of Balfarge, near present day Glenrothes, in Fife, described by one authority as:

‘An illustrious family who, during eleven generations, may be almost said to have established architecture as a profession in Scotland, and passed it to, and maintained it, in a position of dignity and importance to which it had hitherto become a stranger.’

But it was not only through their skills in crafting stone that the Mylnes of Balfarge and their descendants became renowned, but also through their involvement in what today is the worldwide secret brotherhood of Freemasonry.

Masonic architects

The first in a distinguished line of Mylnes who served as Master Mason to the Crown of Scotland – responsible for the building, repair and upkeep of royal residencies and other properties – John Mylne, who died in 1513, was Master Mason to James III.

This was an age when stonemasons employed on building projects were organised into lodges, the name originally given to where they lived, or found lodgings.

In common with other skilled trades, they had their own system of passwords, handshakes and other forms of recognition to guard against outsiders or unskilled masons encroaching on their territory.

But this secret system and its craft gradings of Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason, gradually moved from being the exclusive preserve of working, or operative, stonemasons, to make way for non-operative, or speculative, Freemasons.

A great grandson of the Mylne who served as Master Mason to James III, John Mylne not only served as Master Mason to James VI, but also inducted the king as a Freemason into the Masonic Lodge at Scone, while the Mylnes are also thought to have been responsible for the founding of the Masonic Lodge at Banff.

Made a burgess of Dundee in 1587 for work that included renewal of its harbour, John Mylne was responsible from 1604 to 1617 for the planning and construction of a bridge across the River Tay, at Perth.

He died in 1621 and was buried in the town’s Greyfriars Kirkyard, where a monument was erected to his memory.

His son, also named John, who was born in Perth in 1585, served as Master Mason to the Crown from 1631 until 1636, and was responsible for many works that included a magnificent sundial at Holyrood Palace and work on the royal residence.

A member of the Lodge of Edinburgh and Master of the Lodge of Scone from 1621 to 1627, he died in 1657.

He had resigned his post as Master Mason in 1636 in favour of his son – yet another John – who was born in Perth in1611 and who died in 1667.

A burgess of Edinburgh and a member of the Edinburgh Lodge of Masons, he was responsible for many works throughout the capital, including construction of the Tron Kirk in High Street and repairs to the crown steeple of St Giles.

He was commissioned in 1663 to carry out a detailed survey of the upper floors of Holyrood Palace – and his plans for this, now held in the Bodleian Library of Oxford University, are recognised as Scotland’s earliest surviving architectural drawings.

One of his descendants, Robert Mylne, was the last of the name to hold the post of Master Mason to the Crown, a post he held from 1668 until his death in 1710.

Born in Perth in 1633, he was responsible for the building of a new market cross for the town, in addition to work on Drumlanrig Castle, in Dumfriesshire, and the extension of Wemyss Castle for the Earl of Wemyss.

His busy workload as Master Mason also involved essential repairs to Edinburgh Castle, carried out in 1662, 1677 and 1685, and it was in recognition of this that the castle’s Mylne Battery was named for him.

One of his descendants, also named Robert, was the celebrated architect and civil engineer who was born in Edinburgh in 1733.

After studying architecture in Rome, he returned to Britain and in 1760 won the competition to design the new Blackfriars Bridge across the Thames, in London.

The bridge survived until more than 100 years later, when it had to be replaced after the rebuilding of London Bridge adversely affected the flow of the river.

As surveyor to the New River Company, he was responsible for the supply of drinking water to London’s thirsty thousands, while he also had the onerous responsibility for the maintenance of the magnificent St Paul’s Cathedral.

Back in his native land of Scotland, he built the country house known as Cally, in Galloway, for James Murray of Broughton, and throughout the 1780s and ‘90s designed and laid out the ‘new’ village of Inveraray and remodelled the interior of Inveraray Castle.

Mylne, who died in 1811, was also instrumental in the construction of Lord Nelson’s sarcophagus in the basement of St Paul’s Cathedral.

His second son was the architect and civil engineer William Mylne, born in 1781 and who died in 1863.

Responsible for the design of a number of bridges that included the former Garret Hostel Bridge in Cambridge, he was a member of the elite scientific think-tank, the Royal Society, and a founding member in 1834 of the Institute of British Architects.

At sea, Alfred Mylne was the Scottish yacht designer who was born in Glasgow in 1872 and died in 1951.

Apprenticed to the shipbuilding firm of Napier, Shanks and Bell, he later worked as a craftsman for George Watson, who designed the royal yacht HMY Britannia and a racing cutter owned by Edward, Prince of Wales.

The talented and creative Mylne branched out on his own, setting up A. Mylne and Company in 1896, while he was involved ten years later in the establishment of the yacht racing handicap rule known as the International Metre Rule.

His yacht designing skills were put to different use during the First World War when his yard at Ardmaleish Point, on the west coast island of Bute, was given over to the production of hulls and components for flying boats.

The yacht design company he founded survives to this day as part of Ace Marine Ltd.

In archaeology, James Miln was the Scottish archeologist and antiquarian who was born in 1881.

He is remembered today for his pioneering excavations on Roman sites in the area of the town of Carnac, in Brittany; following his death in his native Glasgow in 1881, his brother, Robert, established the James Miln Museum in Carnac to house the many artefacts that were uncovered.

It was partly thanks to his rather rebellious nature that Alexander Mylne, born in 1742 in Fochabers, Morayshire, became a wealthy entrepreneur and philanthropist.

Such was the power of the landed gentry in these times that he was actually transported to America after incurring the wrath of the local Duke who employed him as a footman.

This was for the temerity of verbally abusing the duke after he had ordered him to cut his long and unruly red hair.

But Scotland’s loss was America’s gain as Mylne established a business empire in New Orleans that, by the time of his death in 1838, had left him immensely wealthy.

Not forgetting his roots, he left money for the establishment of Milne’s Free School, also known as Mylne’s Institution, in Fochabers, while the resort town that he developed on the south shore of Lake Pontchartrain, New Orleans, was named Milneburg in his honour.

name: Paton
history_english:
Ancient bloodlines

A name with a number of what remain rather obscure points of origin, ‘Paton’ and its equally close spelling variant of ‘Patton’ have been present in the British Isles from the earliest times although, in common with many other surnames, it was not popularised until following the Norman Conquest of 1066.

A topographic surname, ‘Paton’ is thought to have originally indicated someone who lived near a landscape feature that may have been stream or a hill or even a prominent structure such as a church.

Originally a forename – in common with many other popular surnames of today – it’s Gaelic Irish form is ‘O’Peatain,’ meaning ‘son of Patrick’, and anglicised as ‘Peyton.’

But it is as ‘Paton’ and ‘Patton’ that the name has stamped indelible marks on the historical record.

This is a record that stretches back through the dim mists of time – meaning that flowing through the veins of many bearers of the names today may well be the blood of those Germanic tribes who invaded and settled in the south and east of the island of Britain from about the early fifth century.

Known as the Anglo-Saxons, they were composed of the Jutes, from the area of the Jutland Peninsula in modern Denmark, the Saxons from Lower Saxony, in modern Germany and the Angles from the Angeln area of Germany.

It was the Angles who gave the name ‘Engla land’, or ‘Aengla land’ – better known as ‘England.’

They held sway in what became England from approximately 550 to 1066, with the main kingdoms those of Sussex, Wessex, Northumbria, Mercia, Kent, East Anglia and Essex.

Whoever controlled the most powerful of these kingdoms was tacitly recognised as overall ‘king’ – one of the most noted being Alfred the Great, King of Wessex from 871 to 899.

It was during his reign that the famous Anglo-Saxon Chronicle was compiled – an invaluable source of Anglo-Saxon history – while Alfred was designated in early documents as Rex Anglorum Saxonum, King of the English Saxons.

Other important Anglo-Saxon works include the epic Beowulf and the seventh century Caedmon’s Hymn.

Through the Anglo-Saxons, the language known as Old English developed, later transforming from the eleventh century into Middle English – sources from which many popular English surnames of today, such as Paton, derive.

The Anglo-Saxons meanwhile, had usurped the power of the indigenous Britons – who referred to them as ‘Saeson’ or ‘Saxones.’

It is from this that the Scottish Gaelic term for ‘English people’ of ‘Sasannach’ derives, the Irish Gaelic ‘Sasanach’ and the Welsh ‘Saeson.’

Of Celtic pedigree, these early Britons were settled for centuries from a line south of the River Forth in Scotland all the way down to the south coast of England and with a particular presence in Wales.

Speaking a Celtic language known as Brythonic, they boasted a glorious culture that flourished even after the Roman invasion of Britain in 43 AD and the subsequent consolidation of Roman power by about 84 AD.

With many of the original Britons absorbing aspects of Roman culture, they became ‘Romano-British’ – while still retaining their own proud Celtic heritage.

We learn from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle how the religion of the early Anglo-Saxons was one that pre-dated the establishment of Christianity in the British Isles. Known as a form of Germanic paganism, with roots in Old Norse religion, it shared much in common with the Druidic ‘nature-worshipping’ religion of the indigenous Britons.

It was in the closing years of the sixth century that Christianity began to take a hold in Britain, while by approximately 690 it had become the ‘established’ religion of Anglo-Saxon England.

The first serious shock to Anglo-Saxon control came in 789 in the form of sinister black-sailed Viking ships that appeared over the horizon off the island monastery of Lindisfarne, in the northeast of the country.

The monastery was sacked in an orgy of violence and plunder, setting the scene for what would be many more terrifying raids on the coastline of not only England, but also those of Wales, Ireland and Scotland.

But the Vikings, or ‘Northmen’, in common with the Anglo-Saxons of earlier times, were raiders who eventually stayed – establishing, for example, what became Jorvik, or York, and the trading port of Dublin, in Ireland.

Through intermarriage, the bloodlines of the Anglo-Saxons also became infused with that of the Vikings.

But there would be another infusion of the blood of the ‘Northmen’ in the wake of the Norman Conquest of 1066 – a key event in English history that sounded the death knell of Anglo-Saxon supremacy.

By this date, England had become a nation with several powerful competitors to the throne.

In what were extremely complex family, political and military machinations, the monarch was Harold II, who had succeeded to the throne following the death of Edward the Confessor.

But his right to the throne was contested by two powerful competitors – his brother-in-law King Harold Hardrada of Norway, in alliance with Tostig, Harold II’s brother, and Duke William II of Normandy.

In what has become known as The Year of Three Battles, Hardrada invaded England and gained victory over the English king on September 20 at the battle of Fulford, in Yorkshire.

Five days later, however, Harold II decisively defeated his brother-in-law and brother at the battle of Stamford Bridge.

But he had little time to celebrate his victory, having to immediately march south from Yorkshire to encounter a mighty invasion force, led by Duke William of Normandy, that had landed at Hastings, in East Sussex.

Harold’s battle-hardened but exhausted force of Anglo-Saxon soldiers confronted the Normans on October 14 in a battle subsequently depicted on the Bayeux tapestry – a 23ft. long strip of embroidered linen thought to have been commissioned eleven years after the event by the Norman Odo of Bayeux.

Harold drew up a strong defensive position at the top of Senlac Hill, building a shield wall to repel Duke William’s cavalry and infantry.

The Normans suffered heavy losses, but through a combination of the deadly skill of their archers and the ferocious determination of their cavalry they eventually won the day.

Anglo-Saxon morale had collapsed on the battlefield as word spread through the ranks that Harold had been killed – the Bayeux Tapestry depicting this as having happened when the English king was struck by an arrow to the head.

Amidst the carnage of the battlefield, it was difficult to identify him – the last of the Anglo-Saxon kings.

Some sources assert William ordered his body to be thrown into the sea, while others state it was secretly buried at Waltham Abbey.

What is known with certainty, however, is that William in celebration of his great victory founded Battle Abbey, near the site of the battle, ordering that the altar be sited on the spot where Harold was believed to have fallen.

William was declared King of England on December 25, and the complete subjugation of his Anglo-Saxon subjects followed.

Those Normans who had fought on his behalf were rewarded with the lands of Anglo-Saxons, many of whom sought exile abroad as mercenaries.

Within an astonishingly short space of time, Norman manners, customs and law were imposed on England – laying the basis for what subsequently became established ‘English’ custom and practice.

But beneath the surface, old Anglo-Saxon culture was not totally eradicated, with some aspects absorbed into those of the Normans, while faint echoes of the Anglo-Saxon past is still seen today in the form of popular surnames such as Paton and Patton.

A family of Normans who had fought on Duke William’s behalf at the battle of Hastings, later adopted the name of Paton – rather confusingly from their manorial estate known as ‘Patton’, in the English county of Shropshire – while others who came to bear the name were to be found throughout the length and breadth of not only the British Isles but also much further afield.

Battle honours

Bearers of the Paton and Patton names name have gained distinction through a range of endeavours, not least through engagement on the bloody field of battle.

Two bearers of the Paton name were recipients of the Victoria Cross (VC), the highest award for valour in the face of enemy action for British and Commonwealth forces.

Born in Stirling in 1833, John Paton was a Scottish recipient of the honour during the Indian Mutiny of 1857 to 1858.

This was an insurrection against British rule that was sparked off through a number of volatile issues including the concerns by the Indian soldiers under British rule, known as sepoys, that cow-fat and pig-fat, anathema to the religions of Hindus and Muslims, was being used to grease the rifle cartridges they were issued.

John Paton had been a sergeant in the 93rd Regiment of Foot – later The Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders – when he performed the actions for which he was awarded the VC. This was at the Siege of Lucknow in November of 1857 when, under heavy enemy fire, he managed to find a breach in their defences and lead his comrades on to capture an important position.

He died in 1914, while his VC is now on display at the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders Museum in Stirling Castle.

Another Scottish recipient of the VC was George Paton, born in 1895 in Inellan, Argyllshire.

This was during the First World War when, as a captain in the 4th Battalion, Grenadier Guards, at Gonnelieu, France, in 1917, he braved devastating enemy fire to take a number of wounded comrades back to his own lines – being mortally wounded after he had successfully done so.

His VC is now on display at The Guards Regimental Headquarters (Grenadier Guards RHQ) at Wellington Barracks, London.

Described by his German counterparts at the end of the Second World War as one of the finest commanders the Allies had had, George Smith Patton, Jr., better known as General George Patton and by his nickname of “Old Blood and Guts”, is remembered for his command of the Seventh United States Army and then the Third United States Army in the European theatre of operations.

Born into a wealthy Virginia family in 1885 and attending both the Virginia Military Institute and the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, he went on to become a leading exponent of the doctrine of armoured warfare – employing this to great effect following the Allied invasion of Normandy in June of 1944.

A keen horseman and athlete, participating in the pentathlon at the 1922 Olympics, in the years following the end of the First World War – when he saw action with the United States Tanks Corps of the American expeditionary Force – he developed the M1913 “Patton Sabre” tank.

Continually pushing his doctrine of armoured warfare on his military superiors during the interwar years, he was placed in command of the U.S. 2nd Armored Division following America’s entry into the Second World War.

Leading American troops in the invasion of Casablanca during the North African Campaign in 1942, he later commanded the Seventh Army during the invasion of Sicily – becoming the subject of controversy when he slapped two soldiers under his command for what he perceived as their lack of moral fibre.

The incident made newspaper headlines and Patton was forced to apologise – returning to the field of battle in command of the Third Army following the Normandy Invasion and leading a daring and rapid armoured drive across France.

During the battle of the Bulge later in 1944, he led the relief of beleaguered American troops at Bastogne, and advanced with the Third Army into Germany.

A highly colourful and controversial figure who was frequently a thorn in the flesh of his superiors, he was nevertheless tolerated because of his undoubted military skills.

Placed for a time at the end of the war as military governor of Bavaria, he died following an automobile accident in December of 1945 while on a pheasant hunting trip in Bavaria.

This occurred when his staff car was struck by a U.S. truck while stationary at a railway crossing.

Taken to hospital for treatment for severe head and spinal injuries, he died twelve days later.

Portrayed by the actor George C. Scott in the 1970 film Patton, he was also the father of the equally distinguished General George Smith Patton, IV.

Born in 1923 and graduating from West Point in 1946, he was stationed for a time in occupied Germany while, in 1953, he was placed in command of “A” Company of the 104th Tank Battalion, 40th Infantry Division – receiving both the Silver Star and the Purple Heart.

Serving throughout the 1960s in Vietnam, he was awarded two Distinguished Service Crosses for his actions on the battlefield, while he also acted for a time as Chief of Operations and Plans at Headquarters, United States Army Vietnam.

Promoted to brigadier general in June of 1970 and placed in command of the U.S. 2nd Armored Division, which his father had commanded for a time during the Second World War, he died in 2004.

Born in 1905 on the Channel island of Jersey, Sir Thomas Paton was the leading British civil engineer whose company played a vital role in the Allied invasion of Hitler’s “Fortress Europe.”

This was through the construction of the precast concrete structures known as caissons used in the Mulberry Harbours that were able to accommodate the transport from ships to the Normandy beaches of vital supplies of fuel, food and munitions for the Allied troops.

He was also responsible for the design of a number of Royal Ordnance factories throughout the United Kingdom, through the company of Sir Alexander Gibb and Partners that his family had founded.

Before his death in 1999 he was the recipient of a number of honours and awards that included a knighthood, Fellowship of the Institution of Structural Engineers and the American Society of Civil Engineers and also of the Royal Society.

Away from the battlefield, Joan Burton Paton was the leading Australian naturalist, environmentalist and ornithologist born in 1916.

Appointed a Member of the Order of Australia four years before her death in 2000 for her services to the environment and ornithology, and a lecturer in ornithology in South Australia’s Workers’ Educational Association, she was also the first woman to be elected to the exclusive Adelaide Ornithologists Club – serving as its president from 1991 to 1993.

name: Williamson
history_scottish:
Royal and ancient

Denoting ‘son of William’, ‘Williamson’ is ranked at 89 in the list of the 100 most common surnames in Scotland, while it is the third most common surname in England.

Derived from the equally popular forename of William, it has truly warlike connotations, stemming as it does from the Germanic ‘will’ and ‘helmet’, as in an armoured helmet worn on the battlefield.

Popularised in England after William the Conqueror’s Norman invasion of 1066, its popularity in Scotland is attributable to the mid-twelfth to early thirteenth century reign of the Scots monarch William the Lyon.

The name, however, was already present in Scotland before the advent of either William the Conqueror or William the Lion – a presence that may come as a surprise to bearers of the name today because it has firm roots in ancient and royal Celtic tradition.

This is through the Gaelic name form of Mac Mhic Uileim, or MacWilliam, the name designation of a distinguished royal dynasty that was brutally extinguished in the early thirteenth century.

Of the Scottish Royal House of Duncan II and with Badenoch and Lochaber as their main territory, the MacWilliams periodically rose up in revolt, claiming a right to the throne.

But it was during the reign of William the Lion’s successor, Alexander II, that their ambitions were finally and bloodily quashed.

By 1229, the sole remaining heir of the MacWilliams was the infant daughter of their Chief, who had been killed in battle, and the medieval Lanercost Chronicle relates how she was put to death in a manner considered horrific for even those particularly brutal times.

The Chronicle states:

MacWilliam’s daughter, who had not long left her mother’s womb, innocent as she was, was put to death, in the burgh of Forfar, in view of the market place, after a proclamation by the public crier.

Her head was struck against the column of the market cross, and her brains dashed out.

By such means, Alexander II not only finally crushed the MacWilliam threat to his throne, but also managed to nearly totally expunge their very name from the Scottish historical record.

However, bloodied but unbowed, bearers of the name, in later spelling variations that include Williamson, managed against all odds to not only survive but also in many cases to thrive and make their personal mark on the pages of the vibrant drama that is Scotland’s turbulent history.

In addition to their own very personal heritage and traditions that include the motto of ‘A little by degrees’ and crest of a sheaf of wheat, the Williamsons of today, as a sept, or sub-branch, of Clan Gunn, are also entitled to share in their traditions.

With their main territories in the far north of Scotland, encompassing Sutherland, Caithness and the Orkney Islands, the ancient Clan Gunn claims descent from Sweyn Asleifsson, also colourfully known as The Ultimate Viking.

It is through his grandson, Gunni, that the clan, whose motto is ‘In peace, in war’ and crest a hand clutching a sword, takes its name – with ‘Gunni’ an Old Norwegian word indicating ‘war’ or ‘battle’.

The Gunns and their kinsfolk such as the Williamsons, Jamiesons, Robinsons and others were for centuries engaged in vicious clan warfare with their territorial rivals the Keiths.

They met in combat in 1438 at the battle of Blare-tannie, in Caithness.

This was a conflict in which the Keiths, supported by their allies the Mackays, emerged victorious – albeit with great slaughter on both sides.

Twenty-six years later, in 1464, the chiefs of the Gunns and the Keiths agreed to meet at the chapel of St Tears, near Girginhoe, Caithness, in a bid to settle their centuries-old differences.

The agreement was that ‘twelve horses from each side’, implying that the chiefs would each be accompanied by no more than twelve horsed warriors, should meet for trial by combat.

But an outnumbered Gunn contingent was slaughtered when the Keiths arrived with two men to each of their twelve horses.

The Gunns never forgot this act of treachery and, 70 years later, they exacted a belated revenge by killing George Keith, Chief of the Keiths, and twelve of his clansmen.

In the much more peaceful times of the 1970s, however, representatives of both clans met at St Tears to sign a Bond of Covenant and Friendship.

This was in 1978, symbolically bringing to an end a bitter feud whose roots lay in the dim and very distant past.

As a sept of the Gunns, the Williamsons of today are also entitled to wear their tartan.

The Gunns and their kinsfolk such as the Williamsons were also members of the mighty confederation of clans known as Clan Chattan, which until as late as the eighteenth century was the main power in the Badenoch region of Speyside.

With its motto of ‘Touch not the cat without a glove’, and crest of a rampant wildcat, Clan Chattan also included within its ranks the Shaws, Mackintoshes, MacPhersons, Farquharsons, MacThomases, McBains, Macleans, McGillivrays and Davidsons.

In Lowland Scotland, one of the most colourful bearers of the Williamson name, in what was otherwise a particularly dark and bloody period of the nation’s turbulent history, was the Covenanting Church of Scotland minister David Williamson – renowned in ballad as ‘Dainty Davie.’

A National Covenant, pledging defence of the Presbyterian religion, had been signed in the Greyfriars Kirkyard, Edinburgh, in February of 1638, about eight years after he was born.

Copies were circulated throughout Scotland, and the hundreds of ordinary men and women who subscribed to it, then and later, became known as Covenanters.

Following the restoration to the throne of Charles II in 1660, the death knell for the Covenanting movement was sounded when a Recissory Act was passed, declaring the Covenant illegal.

Episcopal rule was foisted on the Scottish Church, and all ministers who refused to adhere to this new order were deprived of their parishes.

Along with their congregations, many ministers literally took to the hills, preaching at open-air meetings known as conventicles.

Lookouts were posted to keep a wary eye out for the approach of Government troops, known as dragoons, and justice was executed on the spot for those unfortunate enough to fall into their hands.

Constantly persecuted by the forces of authority, the Covenanters rose in futile rebellion in November of 1666 and, as a sign of the harsh treatment that was to be subsequently meted out to them, many of the prisoners taken were tortured and hanged.

A Covenanting victory was achieved at the battle of Drumclog in June of 1679, only to be followed a few short weeks later by resounding defeat at the battle of Bothwell Brig, near Hamilton, by a force commanded by the Duke of Monmouth.

Nearly 800 Covenanters were killed and 1,400 taken prisoner.

Five years before the battle of Drumclog, David Williamson had been minister of St Cuthbert’s Church, Edinburgh, but was denounced as a rebel for having held conventicles.

Forfeiting his official ministerial charge, he was allowed to return in 1687 following the granting of reprieves known as Indulgences, but was denounced yet again three years later as a Covenanting rebel.

Pursued by the authorities, he found shelter in the homes of a number of Covenanting sympathisers.

These included the Kerr family of Cherrytrees, near Leith.

As dragoons approached their home, where Williamson had found refuge, Lady Cherrytrees put him in bed dressed in women’s nightclothes beside her daughter Jane – passing him off to the dragoons as her daughter’s ‘bedmate.’

This was a ruse to which Williamson is said to have ‘modestly and readily consented’, and while Lady Cherrytrees entertained the unsuspecting dragoons to food and drink, the bold Covenanter took full and lascivious advantage of the situation in which he found himself by getting his ‘bedmate’ pregnant.

He subsequently married her, making her the second of the eight wives he had before his death in 1706, the father of at least nine children.

His pre-marital escapade with Jane Kerr became the subject of the ballad Dainty Davie, one of the many later collected for posterity by Scotland’s national bard Robert Burns, and one verse of which reads:

When he was chased by a dragoon,
Into my bed he was laid doon,
I thought him worthy o’ his room,
And he’s aye my Dainty Davie.

Chains and slavery

For a nation whose forebears have frequently fought and died in the cause of freedom, it comes as something of a shock to learn that parents once lived in terror of their young sons being kidnapped from their native Scotland and sold into slavery.

It was in 1760 that a 30-year-old man, Peter Williamson, arrived in Scotland from the American colonies with a rather odd and disturbing tale to relate – one that would later provide some of the inspiration for Robert Louis Stevenson’s novel Kidnapped.

His claim was that he had been kidnapped in Aberdeen and sold into slavery on the American plantations nearly twenty years earlier.

In 1762, after publishing an account of his kidnap and subsequent adventures in America, French and American Cruelty; exemplified in the life and various vicissitudes of fortune of Peter Williamson, he raised a civil action against the Burgh of Aberdeen, accusing it of culpability in allowing him to be kidnapped by agents of William Fordyce, an Aberdeen merchant and magistrate.

Williamson was imprisoned for a time in Aberdeen on libel charges, but later won his civil action and £100 in damages.

He had been born in 1730 in the parish of Aboyne, Aberdeenshire, where his father was a tenant farmer.

Aged ten, he was sent to school in Aberdeen, where he lived with an aunt.

His civil action chillingly relates how at that time it was a common and well-known practice among the merchants of Aberdeen and other areas to pick up young, healthy, boys from the streets and surrounding countryside.

They were confined in barns and other convenient out of the way places until such time as a sufficient number of them were gathered.

In what proved to be lucrative ‘trade’ for the merchants and their associates, they were then packed aboard a vessel to be sold as slaves on the plantations of America or the West Indies.

This was Peter Williamson’s heart-rending fate.

His civil action states how “it was the misfortune of the Pursuer to fall into the hands of one employed by Bailie William Fordyce and Company, merchants in Aberdeen, to pick up boys.”

Plucked from the streets along with a number of other young lads, he was held in a building owned by rich merchants before, in July of 1743, being put aboard a vessel bound for America.

Locked below decks, he found himself in the company of 67 other unfortunate boys who had either been taken from the streets or from the surrounding countryside.

The vessel, Planter, docked in Philadelphia after a voyage of nearly three months, and where the bewildered lads were sold off to local farmers and merchants.

Bought by a farmer who had also arrived in America from Scotland as a slave but who had been able to regain his freedom, Williamson was fortunate in that he also later managed to secure his freedom.

But he became a victim of the savage battles waged against the Indian and French forces then in the colonies – with the woman he had married being killed and he for a time being held a captive of Delaware Indians.

Following his return to his native land and his ultimately successful action against the Burgh of Aberdeen, he opened a coffee shop in Edinburgh’s Parliament House.

He became a well-known figure, fondly known as Indian Peter because of his custom of parading through the city streets colourfully dressed in Native Indian costume.

Responsible for the compilation of Edinburgh’s first street directory, he also introduced the Penny Post system to the city.

He died in 1799 and waas laid to rest in Old Calton Cemetery – dressed in his Native Indian costume.

Another Scottish bearer of the Williamson name who lived through rather unusual times in America was John Williamson, a noted political radical who was born in Glasgow.

Immigrating to the United States as a young man, he joined the Communist Party of America in 1922, becoming active in its youth wing, and two years later attending the 4th World Congress of the Young Communist International, in Moscow.

In 1949, during the period of the ‘Red Scare’ that swept America, he was among a number of leading American Communists who were arrested and imprisoned.

He was immediately deported to Britain after serving a five-year term in prison.

Becoming a prominent member of the Communist Party of Great Britain, he died in 1974.

In battle, John Leon Williamson, born in 1921 in Ash, North Carolina, was the U.S. Navy Seaman First Class who was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross.

He had survived action, aboard the U.S.S. fighting cruiser Raleigh, during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7th, 1941, but was later killed while manning a gun during the assault on Guadalcanal in November of the following year.

It was for this action that he was awarded the Navy Cross, while the U.S. Navy vessel John L. Williamson was named in his honour.

name: Buchan
history_legacy:
Clan Buchan take their name from the district of Buchan in Aberdeenshire. Originally used by the earls, it later became a name used by any notable inhabitants of the region.

The name is first recorded in the thirteenth century, but it is believed that the lands of Auchmacoy did not come into the hands of the Buchans until the early 16th century, when Andrew Buchan received a charter to the lands from King James IV.

The Buchans of Auchmacoy was loyal to the royal family and the House of Stewart. Thomas Buchan, third son of clan chief James Buchan, was appointed as commander-in-chief of the Jacobite forces in Scotland in 1689. After being defeated at the Battle of Cromdale in 1690, Buchan joined forces with the Farquharsons and marched on Aberdeen, tricking the opposition forces into thinking they were grossly outnumbed. Despite forcing a retreat, they were eventually intercepted by General Mackay's government forces and Buchan's troops dispersed. He was sent to exile in France, but continued to communicate with the royal family until his death in 1721.

Today the clan seat is still in place in Auchmacoy. The Buchan clan motto is "Non Inferiora Secutus" (Following Not the Inferior) and the clan crest is a sunflower turning towards the sun.

name: Chalmers
history_scottish:
Martyrs of the Covenant

Proud bearers of the surname of Chalmers, or Chambers, may be pleasantly surprised to learn that their name has distinctly regal connotations, stemming as it does from the trusted office of chamberlain, who was in charge of the ‘chamber’, or exchequer, into which royal revenues were paid.

Of Anglo-Saxon origin, variations include Chaumers, Chamber, and Chamberlain, with Chalmers being the Scottish form of the common English form of Chambers.

Both names, however, have flourished in Scotland over the centuries.

The process whereby nobles paid money into the royal exchequer in return for the lands they held was known in Latin as paying ‘in cameran’, while the ‘camerarius’, or ‘chamberlain’, was in charge of this often complex process.

A grandly named Herbertus, who held lands in both Lanarkshire and Ayrshire, is recorded as the Camerarius Regis Scotiae, or Great Chamberlain of Scotland, during the reign from 1124 to 1153 of Scotland’s David I.

One of his descendants, James Chalmers of Gadgirth, was a fiery Protestant reformer whose zeal was much admired and remarked on by the great father of the Reformation John Knox.

Chalmers even went as far as berating the regent Mary of Guise herself in an infamous public confrontation in 1558.

A Robert de la Chaumbre is recorded in 1296, while an Alexander of Chamour is recorded in 1461 in Aberdeen, and it is in Aberdeenshire that the families of Chalmers of Balnacraig, Cults, and Albar flourished for centuries, while there were also prominent families of the name in Ayrshire.

In addition to the Protestant reformer James Chalmers of Gadgirth, a number of Chalmers also figure prominently in the annals of Scotland’s often bitter religious history.

Robert Chalmers was one of five men from the parish of Shotts, in Lanarkshire, who were among 201 Covenanter prisoners who drowned while being transported to Barbados to be sold as slaves after being captured at the battle of Bothwell Brig.

A National Covenant, pledging defence of the Presbyterian religion, had been signed in the Greyfriars Kirk, in Edinburgh, in February of 1638. Copies were circulated throughout the length and breadth of Scotland, and the hundreds of ordinary folk who signed it, such as Robert Chalmers, were known as Covenanters.

Episcopal rule was foisted on the Scottish Church following the Restoration of Charles II in 1660, and ministers who refused to abide by this were deprived of their parishes.

The Covenanters rose in rebellion in November of 1666 and many of the prisoners taken were tortured and hanged.

Victory for the Covenanters came at the battle of Drumclog in June of 1679, only to be followed a few short weeks later by defeat at the battle of Bothwell Brig, near Hamilton.

Nearly 800 Covenanters were killed, and 1,400 taken prisoner. Kept for several weeks in open cages in the Greyfriars Kirkyard, those who agreed to sign a bond for future ‘good behaviour’ were released, but by November of 1679, a number of prisoners, including Robert Chalmers, still remained.

The authorities decided to sell them as slaves on the plantations of Barbados, and 250 of them, including Chalmers, were packed aboard the Crown of London, which set sail from Leith on November 27.

Battling ferocious winter storms, the Crown of London sailed up the east coast of Scotland, finally being forced to anchor for safety off the headland of Scarva Taing, near the Mull Head of Deerness, in Orkney.

Disaster struck as the ship’s anchor snapped in the raging torrents and the vessel was driven onto rocks. The crew managed to escape, but the captain ordered that the hatches securing the prisoners below decks remained locked.

About fifty prisoners did manage to make it to land, however, but as they attempted to claw their way to safety up the steep cliff face they were callously pushed back down onto the jagged rocks and into the raging sea on the orders of the captain.

More than 200 bodies were later washed up on the Deerness coastline.

The uncompromising stance taken on matters of religion by Covenanting martyrs such as Robert Chalmers was also taken up in later centuries by Dr Thomas Chalmers, the preacher, theologian, and economist who was born in Anstruther, Fife, in 1780.

Regarded as the most influential preacher of the nineteenth century, he was appointed professor of divinity at Edinburgh University in 1843, and following what is known as the ‘Disruption’ of the Church of Scotland in 1843, he became a founder of the Free Church of Scotland and its first Moderator.

While there is a Chalmers family motto of ‘Advance’, and a crest of the head and neck of a lion, bearers of the name are also recognised as a sept, or branch, of the proud Clan Cameron, and any Chalmers of today who can trace a descent back to the ancient Cameron homeland of Lochaber are entitled to share in the clan’s motto of ‘Unite’, its crest of a sheaf of five arrows, and adopt its tartan.

A rather curious tradition relates to how bearers of the surname Chalmers became a sept of the clan – a tradition that has its roots in the fact that many Scots, particularly the sons of noble families, entered the military service of successive French monarchs.

One of these was a Cameron who took the Latin name of Camerarius, or Camerario, as ‘being more agreeable to the language of that country’: in French, this translated as ‘de la Chambre’, or ‘Chalmers/Chambers’.

When he returned to Scotland (although some sources state it was his son), the name was retained, and so was later founded the ‘dynasty’ of the Chalmers of Aberdeenshire.

This Chalmers link to Clan Cameron makes them heirs to a proud, but often bloody, tradition.

For the Jacobite cause

Clan Cameron had for centuries held lands in the Lochaber region, mainly around Loch Lochy, and it was a Sir John de Cameron who in 1321 was one of the signatories of that resounding clarion call of Scotland’s freedom known as the Declaration of Arbroath.

Ninety years later, the Camerons and their kinsfolk such as the Chalmers took part in one of the most savage battles on Scottish soil, the battle of Harlaw, fought on July 24, 1411.

Also known as the Battle of Red Harlaw because of the blood spilled, no side emerged victorious.

Donald MacDonald, 2nd Lord of the Isles, had mustered about 6000 of his best clansmen and burned Inverness after crossing to the mainland and marching up the Great Glen.

His strength swelled to 10,000 after other clansmen including Camerons, Chattans, MacIntoshes, and MacLeods joined him. Promising them rich pickings, MacDonald marched them towards Aberdeen.

The Earl of Mar hastily assembled a force that included northeast lairds while the Provost of Aberdeen also raised men.

The opposing forces met just north of Aberdeen, and battle was joined shortly after the summer sun had risen.

The fearless and ferocious clansmen repeatedly charged the ranks of the Earl of Mar and his men, only to be cut down in swathes, but not before exacting their own toll in blood.

As the sun sank low in the west, both sides were exhausted and had to retire from the fray, leaving behind a battlefield littered with the corpses of at least 1000 clansmen and 600 of Mar’s men.

Chalmerses were also among the Cameron kinsfolk who fought under the colours of Sir Ewen Cameron of Lochiel, 17th Chief of Clan Cameron, at the battle of Killiecrankie.

Following the ‘Glorious Revolution’ of 1688 that brought William of Orange and his wife Mary to the thrones of England and Scotland, John Graham of Claverhouse, Viscount Dundee, raised the Royal Standard in favour of the exiled Stuart monarch James VII and II.

Gathering a 2,500-strong force of clansmen that included a contingent from Clan Cameron, he engaged a 4000-strong government force under General Hugh Mackay of Scourie at the Pass of Killiecrankie on July 27, 1689.

Brave, but undisciplined, the clansmen fired off a volley of musket fire before throwing the muskets to the ground and rushing pell-mell down hill into Mackay’s closely packed ranks.

The clansmen were mown down in their hundreds by the disciplined musket fire of Mackay’s troopers, but not before inflicting equally heavy losses.

Both sides suffered terribly in the battle and the outcome proved to be inconclusive, but, fatally for the cause of the exiled Stuart king, ‘Bonnie Dundee’ died the next day from his wounds.

Jacobite unrest in Scotland intensified following the Hanoverian succession to the throne under George, Elector of Hanover, in 1714, and in September of the following year John, the 11th Earl of Mar, raised the Standard of James VIII and III, the ‘Old Pretender’, at Braemar.

Mar raised an impressive force that included Camerons under the leadership of John, the son of the 17th chief who had fought at Killiecrankie.

The Jacobite ranks were plagued by bad leadership and lack of a coherent strategy, however, and the cause was effectively lost following the battle of Sheriffmuir on November 13, after Mar lost the initiative by withdrawing north to Perth.

The Old Pretender landed at Peterhead in December, later travelling to Perth where he held a dispirited court for three weeks before departing for foreign shores, never to return.

It was Donald Cameron, known to posterity as ‘the Gentle Lochiel’, and whose father had fought for the Old Pretender, who let his heart rule his head and, against his better judgement, supported the doomed cause of the Young Pretender, Prince Charles Edward Stuart, during the abortive Jacobite Rising of 1745 to 1746.

The prince had landed on the small Outer Hebridean island of Eriskay on July 22, 1745, landing on the mainland at Loch nan Uamh three days later.

It was vital for him to receive the armed support of the powerful clan chiefs in his quest to restore the Royal House of Stuart to the throne, and one of his first visitors was the Gentle Lochiel.

Although Lochiel welcomed his prince with all due respect, he informed him that without an army at his back he should never have come.

The angry prince is said to have retorted: ‘In a few days, with the few friends that I have, I will erect the royal standard and proclaim to the people of Britain that Charles Stuart is come over to claim the crown of his ancestors, to win it or perish in the attempt’, adding that Lochiel could stay at home and learn the fate of his prince from the newspapers.

His Highland pride stung by this, Lochiel replied: ‘No! I will share the fate of my prince and so shall every man over whom nature or fortune has given me any power!’

The Jacobite Standard was raised a few weeks later, on August 19, at Glenfinnan, on Loch Shiel, and Lochiel and his 800 clansmen and kinsfolk were among the first to rally to it.

It is also known that Chalmers was a ‘code-name’ for many Camerons during the Rising, and they were destined to pay a bloody price for their support, however, when Jacobite hopes were dashed forever at the battle of Culloden, fought on Drummossie Moor, near Inverness, on April 16, 1746.

In what was the last major battle fought on British soil, hundreds of clansmen died on the battlefield while hundreds of others died later from their wounds and the brutal treatment of their government captors.

The Muster Roll for the Jacobite army records that four men of the name of Chalmers, including two ploughmen, served in the Forfarshire (Ogilvy’s) Regiment, while Francis Chalmers was a servant to Lord George Murray, the prince’s Lieutenant General.

Charles Chalmers, a merchant from Edinburgh, served in Elcho and Balmerino’s Lifeguards, while William Chalmers served under the colours of the Duke of Perth’s Regiment and John Chalmers served with the Irish Picquets.

Less than a century later, bearers of the name of Chalmers were still to be found on the battlefield, and one of the most prominent of them was Major General Sir William Chalmers, of Glenericht, in Perthshire.

Born in 1787, he entered army service at the age of 16, and by the time of the battle of Waterloo in 1815 he was in command of a wing of the 52nd Foot.

A redoubtable warrior who was always found in the thick of battle, he is reckoned to have had nine horses killed or wounded under him during his military career – three of them at Waterloo alone.

Far from the battlefield, however, proud bearers of the name of Chalmers and Chambers have achieved distinction in a wide variety of rather more peaceful pursuits.

name: Mills
history_english:
Fields of battle

Both an occupational and a locational surname, ‘Mills’ derives, via the Anglo-Saxons, from the Old English ‘mylen’, meaning ‘mill’ – such as a corn mill – and originally indicated someone who either worked in such a place or lived near one.

The surname ‘Miller’ or ‘Millar’, meanwhile, specifically indicated someone who worked in, or operated, a mill.

Ranked at 94th in some lists of the 100 most common surnames in England, ‘Mills’ is of truly ancient roots.

With an Anglo-Saxon pedigree, this means that flowing through the veins of many bearers of the name today may well be the blood of those Germanic tribes who invaded and settled in the south and east of the island of Britain from about the early fifth century.

Known as the Anglo-Saxons, they were composed of the Jutes, from the area of the Jutland Peninsula in modern Denmark, the Saxons from Lower Saxony, in modern Germany and the Angles from the Angeln area of Germany.

It was the Angles who gave the name ‘Engla land’, or ‘Aengla land’ – better known as ‘England.’

They held sway in what became England from approximately 550 to 1066, with the main kingdoms those of Sussex, Wessex, Northumbria, Mercia, Kent, East Anglia and Essex.

Whoever controlled the most powerful of these kingdoms was tacitly recognised as overall ‘king’ – one of the most noted being Alfred the Great, King of Wessex from 871 to 899.

It was during his reign that the famous Anglo-Saxon Chronicle was compiled – an invaluable source of Anglo-Saxon history – while Alfred was designated in early documents as Rex Anglorum Saxonum, King of the English Saxons.

Other important Anglo-Saxon works include the epic Beowulf and the seventh century Caedmon’s Hymn.

Through the Anglo-Saxons, the language known as Old English developed, later transforming from the eleventh century into Middle English – sources from which many popular English surnames of today, such as Mills, derive.

But the death knell of Anglo-Saxon supremacy was sounded with the Norman Conquest of 1066 – a key event in English history.

By this date, England had become a nation with several powerful competitors to the throne – and in what were extremely complex family, political and military machinations, the English monarch was Harold II, who had succeeded to the throne following the death of Edward the Confessor.

But his right to the throne was contested by two powerful competitors – his brother-in-law King Harold Hardrada of Norway, in alliance with Tostig, Harold II’s brother, and Duke William II of Normandy.

In what has become known as The Year of Three Battles, Hardrada invaded England and gained victory over the English king on September 20 at the battle of Fulford, in Yorkshire.

Five days later, however, Harold II decisively defeated his brother-in-law and brother at the battle of Stamford Bridge.

But he had little time to celebrate his victory, having to immediately march south from Yorkshire to encounter a mighty invasion force, led by Duke William of Normandy that had landed at Hastings, in East Sussex.

Harold’s battle-hardened but exhausted force of Anglo-Saxon soldiers confronted the Normans on October 14, with Harold drawing up a strong defensive position at the top of Senlac Hill, building a shield wall to repel the duke’s cavalry and infantry.

The Normans suffered heavy losses, but through a combination of the deadly skill of their archers and the ferocious determination of their cavalry they eventually won the day.

Morale had collapsed on the battlefield as word spread through the ranks that Harold had been killed – the last of the Anglo-Saxon kings.

William was declared King of England on December 25, and the complete subjugation of his Anglo-Saxon subjects followed.

Within an astonishingly short space of time, Norman manners, customs and law were imposed on England – laying the basis for what subsequently became established ‘English’ custom and practice.

But beneath the surface, old Anglo-Saxon culture was not totally eradicated, with some aspects absorbed into those of the Normans, while faint echoes of the Anglo-Saxon past is still seen today in the form of surnames such as Mills.

In common with many other English surnames, Mills became popularised in the wake of the Conquest, and a Norman family who later adopted the name were granted lands in Hampshire as a reward for their services at the battle of Hastings.

But it is a name that quickly came to be found throughout the length and breadth of the British Isles, and one which features prominently in the historical record.

On the field of battle, Walter Mills was a posthumous recipient during the First World War of the Victoria Cross (VC), the highest award for valour in the face of enemy action for British and Commonwealth forces.

Born in 1894 in Oldham, Lancashire, he had been a private in C Company, the 1/10th Battalion, The Manchester Regiment, when in December 1917 near Givenchy, France he performed the actions for which he was awarded the honour.

While he was manning a position named Red Dragon Crater, the enemy unleashed a deadly gas attack and then launched an assault on the lines.

Private Mills, despite being gassed, single-handedly lobbed bombs at the infiltrating enemy patrol until reinforcements arrived.

Staying at his post until the enemy was driven off, he died of gas poisoning while being carried to an aid station; his VC was buried with his daughter, Ellen, who died in the 1920s.

Used to great effect by the British Army during the First World War, the Mills bomb, or grenade, was the brainchild of the engineer and inventor William Mills.

Born in 1856 in Southwick, Sunderland, the son of a shipbuilder, he served an apprenticeship with a marine engineering firm before spending seven years at sea and obtaining a first class certificate as a marine engineer in 1884.

While at sea, Mills had become aware of the needless loss of life caused by the unsafe methods used to engage and disengage lifeboats.

Applying his inventive talent to the problem, he devised a simple and safe mechanical method – the Instantaneous Engaging and Disengaging Gear for Ships and Boats – that was first exhibited in 1886 at the Liverpool Ship Owners’ Exhibition.

Gaining the seal of approval of the British Board of Trade, the design became standard throughout the world for not only merchant vessels but also for naval craft.

Establishing the Atlas Works, Britain’s first aluminium foundry, in Bonnersfield, Monkwearmouth, the enterprising Mills, a keen golfer, produced a popular range of aluminium golf clubs.

But it was in 1915 that he opened the Mills Munitions Factory in Birmingham to manufacture what was officially known as the Mills Bomb Hand Grenade.

Up until then, the grenades used since the outbreak of the war in 1914 were cast-iron explosive canisters on an 18-inch long stick, or handle.

These proved as dangerous to those throwing them as to the enemy, because they frequently caught on the front of the trench when lobbed.

Mills solved the problem by inventing a grenade with a spring-loaded firing pin and spring-loaded lever locked by a pin; a four-second time fuse also allowed the grenade thrower to take cover before it exploded.

Honoured with a knighthood in 1922, Mills died ten years later – while one of his last, rather more peaceful, inventions was the telescopic walking stick.

Public service and science

Bearers of the proud name of Mills have gained honours, distinction and renown through a wide range of endeavours and pursuits.

During the Second World War, Percy Herbert Mills, born in 1890 in Thornby on Tees, was the British industrialist and public servant who held the important post of Controller-General of Machine Tools at the Ministry of Supply from 1940 to 1944.

Raised to the Peerage of the United Kingdom in January 1957 as Baron Mills, he was appointed shortly afterwards to the Cabinet of Prime Minister Harold MacMillan as Minister of Power.

Later created Viscount Mills and described as “one of the most politically influential industrialists of all time”, he died in 1968.

Taking to the skies, George Mills, born in 1902 in Dartford, Kent, was the senior Royal Air Force (RAF) commander who served in a number of positions during the Second World War that included command of No. 115 Squadron and Director of Policy (General) at the Air Ministry.

Top level posts he held after the war included Commander Allied Air Forces Central Europe.

A recipient of the Distinguished Flying Cross (DFC), he also served for a time following his retirement from the RAF in 1962 in the ceremonial position of Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod in the Houses of Parliament; he died in 1971.

In the world of politics and the legal profession, Dame Barbara Mills (née Warnock) born in 1940, held a number of senior appointments that included Director of the Serious Fraud Office and Director of Public Prosecutions; appointed a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE), she died in 2011.

Reaching for the heavens, Bernard Mills was the Australian engineer and pioneer of radio astronomy born in 1920, the son of an architect who had emigrated from England.

After studying engineering at Sydney University and later achieving a Master of Engineering degree, he went on to work with Australia’s Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) radio astronomy group.

Responsible for the development of the Mills Cross Telescope, which became operational in 1954 and, twelve years later, the Molonglo Cross Telescope, he died in 2011 – while his many awards included Fellowship of the Australian Academy of Science and of the Royal Society.

Born in 1919, Harlan D. Mills was the pioneering American computer software engineer who, after serving as a bomber pilot during the Second World War, earned a doctorate in mathematics from Iowa State University in 1952.

Working as an IBM research fellow and later professor of computer science at the Florida Institute of Technology, he went on to form the Florida-based company Software Engineering Technology, developing many aspects of software innovation.

The author of a number of books and articles for technical journals on software engineering and known as a ‘super-programmer’, he died in 1996, while three years later the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Computer Society created the Harlan D. Mills Award in his honour.

This is for ‘contributions to the theory and practice of the information sciences focussed on software engineering.’

In the world of the social sciences, Charles Wright Mills, better known as C. Wright Mills, born in 1916 in Waco, Texas, was the leading American political sociologist best known for his 1959 work The Sociological Imagination.

With other important works that include his 1951 White Collar and the 1956 The Power Elite, he died in 1962.

One particularly tragic tale concerning bearers of the Mills name involves Jack Mills, the driver of the Glasgow-London mail train that, in what is known as the Great Train Robbery of August of 1963, was attacked by armed robbers who made off with £2.5million – the equivalent of £41million today.

On the day of the robbery, Mr Mills had boarded the train as relief driver at Crewe station, his home town, in Cheshire.

As he drove the train onwards to Euston station in London, the robbers, who were waiting near Leighton Buzzard, Buckinghamshire, changed a set of signals from green to yellow and then red, forcing the driver to halt.

Mr Mills was attacked with an iron bar after they boarded the train and suffered a black eye and facial bruising, while he and co-driver David Whitby were handcuffed to the engine compartment of their cab.

Mr Mills, aged 57 at the time of the robbery, never fully recovered from the ordeal and after prolonged periods of sick leave was forced to retire four years later.

He had received £250 in compensation for the attack, and there was a public outcry when it was later revealed that Charmian Biggs, the wife of robber Ronnie Biggs, had been paid £65,000 for her story by a Sunday newspaper.

A public appeal launched on the former driver’s behalf by the Daily Mail newspaper raised £34,000, allowing him to move into a more comfortable home.

Mr Mills died in February, 1970.

A coroner gave the cause as chronic lymphatic leukaemia and bronchial pneumonia and, as far as he was concerned, there was no connection between the attack on him seven years earlier and his death.

But debate still rages as to whether or not the attack did indeed affect his health and ability to work.

On a much lighter note, Bertram Mills, born in 1873, was the owner and operator of the famed Bertram Mills Circus.

The son of a funeral director and coach builder based in Paddington, London, he left school when aged 15 and was first employed washing down the horse-drawn coaches for the family funeral business.

Joining the Royal Army Medical Corps on the outbreak of the First World War and attaining the rank of captain, at the end of the conflict he returned to work for the family business for a time.

He became interested, however, in what was then the well-known circus company Wilkins and Young – and placed a bet with a friend that he would form his own circus company and within a year be as successful as them.

True to his word, he formed the Bertram Mills International Circus, and it quickly proved an enormous success.

Particularly popular were his Christmas events at the Olympia in West London – performances that annually attracted not only the general public but also the great and the good such as the Royal Family, Winston Churchill and other dignitaries and celebrities.

He died in 1938 and the circus was taken over by his sons Cyril and Bernard, who ensured its continuing success.

But its popularity dwindled with the advent of television as a stay-at-home form of entertainment, and was finally disbanded in the early 1960s.

name: Docherty
history_scottish:
Of royal race

After Murphy, Docherty is the second most common surname of Irish origin in Scotland: there is nothing common, however, about the proud heritage and traditions of the generations of bearers of the surname who have contributed to the nation’s rich historical tapestry.
