Her life was tragically cut short at the age of 55 when she died from an overdose of barbiturates.

Although her death was officially recorded as accidental, other sources at the time asserted she had committed suicide – relating to problems with her then secret love affair with the married Herbert Morrison.

name: Hill
history_scottish:
Honour bound

A ‘location surname’ in that it originates with reference to someone who lived on a hill or where a hill was a dominant feature of the local landscape, ‘Hill’ is ranked at 30 in the list of the 100 most common surnames in the United Kingdom.

Not specific to any particular region of Scotland, where it is ranked at number 93, it nevertheless appears to have been commonly found in the Lowlands, with bearers of the name not recognised as a sept, or sub-branch, of any particular Scottish clan.

There are, however, a number of Hill family Coats of Arms, with the most common motto recognised as “Advance” and crest of a castellated tower.

In common with several other common surnames found in Scotland, lack of a definite clan connection does not preclude them from having made a significant contribution to the vibrant drama that is the nation’s history.

Scottish bearers of the Hill name were also largely responsible for introducing the name to Ireland, although it is also sometimes found on the island as a variant of the native Irish names Glanney and Glenny.

The introduction of the name to the Emerald Isle from Scotland, mainly to the northern province of Ulster, came about through ‘plantation’.

This was a policy that involved the settlement of loyal Protestants throughout the reigns of England’s Elizabeth I, James I (James VI of Scotland) and Charles I.

One bearer of the Hill name figures in the grim accounts of one of the most notorious incidents in Scotland’s frequently bloody history.

This was the infamous Massacre of Glencoe.

Although a Jacobite rebellion had been quashed in 1689, one year after James II (James VII of Scotland) had fled to exile in France and William of Orange had been invited to take the united thrones of England and Scotland, the Highlands were still in a ferment of unrest.

The problem faced by the authorities was how to quell this unrest and pacify the clans that still adhered to the forlorn Jacobite cause.

A meeting of clan chiefs was convened near Bridge of Orchy, in Perthshire, in June of 1691, and all clans that had fought against the government were granted an amnesty on condition that their chiefs signed a personal oath of allegiance to William, before a magistrate, no later than January 1, 1692.

The Secretary of State for Scotland, Sir John Dalrymple, the Master of Stair, was convinced that not all of the clan chiefs would sign the required oath, and accordingly laid plans to punish those who refused.

As a result of circumstances that were beyond his control, not the least heavy snowfalls that slowed his progress, Alasdair MacIain, the 12th Clan Chief of the Glencoe MacDonalds, was late in meeting the required deadline.

This ominously resulted in his name not being entered on the all-important list of those who had signed.

The Master of Stair saw his opportunity and resolved to make a harsh example of the MacDonalds of Glencoe.

A secret commission to carry this out was given to Captain Robert Campbell of Glenlyon, who took a force of about 140 men to Glencoe, armed with a warrant to quarter them in the homes of the MacDonalds who lived at the bottom of the glen.

Glenlyon and his soldiers spent nearly two weeks enjoying the hospitality of the 500 or so MacDonalds among whom they had been quartered.

Orders finally arrived for Glenlyon to fall upon the unsuspecting MacDonalds and massacre them – sparing no one under the age of 70, women and children not excepted.

The exact figure is not known, but in the early hours of February 13, 1692, at least 38 men, women, and children were slaughtered while countless others died in the severe snowstorm into which they had fled.

MacIain of Glencoe was cold-bloodedly shot as he attempted to rise from his bed.

One of the very few to have played an honourable role in this otherwise sordid affair and to have emerged with his character unblemished, was Colonel John Hill, who served as Governor of Fort William from 1690 to 1698.

Despite the role he played, surprisingly very little biographical detail is available, but what is known is that he was of a family of Hill who owned an estate at Waughton, near East Fortune, and that at the time of the massacre the Scot was also a Lieutenant Colonel in the Earl of Argyle’s Regiment of Foot.

Described by one source as “an honest old soldier”, it was before him that the ill-fated MacDonald appeared at Fort William to take the oath.

But Colonel Hill had to explain to the exhausted Clan Chief that only the sheriff at Inveraray could take it and, sympathising with his plight, provided him with a letter to the sheriff urgently appealing that he be granted some leniency over his late arrival.

Unfortunately this had no effect, and matters proceeded on their grim course.

After the massacre, it was thanks only to Hill that the survivors were pardoned and allowed to return to what remained of their dwellings.

This was because of a personal appeal he made on their behalf to the King.

As the records note: “ … on the solicitation of Colonel Hill, His Majesty granted pardon and remission to the people of Glencoe, allowing them liberty to return and dwell in their old habitations, upon the condition that, for the future, they shall carry themselves peaceably, honestly and abiding by the laws …”

On a much different field of conflict, bearers of the Hill name gained honours and distinction during the American Civil War of 1861 to 1865.

Born in 1825 in Culpeper, Virginia, Ambrose Powell Hill, better known as A.P. Hill, was the Confederate general famed for his command of Hill’s Light Division of the Army of North Virginia.

Distinguishing himself in battles that included Second Bull Run, Antietam and Fredericksburg, he was killed in April 1865 during the siege of Petersburg.

The sword he was wielding when he fell is now on display at the Chesterfield County Museum, Virginia, while Fort A.P. Hill, in Virginia’s Caroline County, is named in his honour.

One of his contemporaries in the Army of North Virginia was the Confederate general Daniel Harvey Hill, better known as D. H. Hill.

Born in 1821 of Scots-Irish stock in York District, South Carolina, he was also a noted scholar.

Surviving the Civil War, he later edited the North Carolina magazine The Land We Love, dealing with historical and social subjects, while he served from 1877 until five years before his death in 1889 as the first president of the University of Arkansas.

Teachers and tycoons

Back in one of the Hill homelands of Scotland, and away from the battlefield, George Hill was the outspoken Church of Scotland minister who held a number of distinguished positions in the religious life of the nation.

Born the son of a minister in St Andrews in 1750 and following in his father’s footsteps by being ordained a minister himself in 1778, he served as Moderator of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland in 1789 and held a number of other positions that included principal of Mary’s College, St Andrews, and Dean of the Chapel Royal, Edinburgh.

Despite his reputation as an ardent British patriot, he was vociferously opposed during the French Revolutionary Wars to a proposal that ministers should preach in support of a financial levy from parishioners in aid of the war effort.

This, he said, would compromise the independence of the Church, and famously declared that, while he would willingly contribute himself, he would “strip the gown from my back rather than obey an order to promote it from the pulpit.” Also a noted teacher and a founding member of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, he died in 1810.

Not only a noted artist but also a pioneer of early photographic techniques, David Octavius Hill was born in 1802 in Perth, the son of a publisher and bookseller.

Educated at Perth Academy and later studying at the School of Design, Edinburgh, where he learned the art of lithography, he first came to attention through his Sketches of Scenery in Perthshire, while The Institution for the Promotion of Fine Arts in Scotland exhibited many of his landscape paintings.

Among a number of Scottish artists who became dissatisfied with the work of the institution, he helped to found an alternative, the Scottish Academy, later the Royal Scottish Academy, in 1829.

In addition to providing illustrations for the works of Robert Burns and Sir Walter Scott, he also collaborated from 1839 with the pioneering photographer Robert Adamson in producing a stunning series of prints that utilised the latter’s skill in photography and Hill’s adeptness in composition.

One of the most famous examples of their collaboration is The Disruption, based on the Disruption Assembly in Edinburgh in 1843 when a number of Church of Scotland ministers walked out of the assembly hall in protest and founded the Free Church of Scotland.

Hill and Adamson are also famed for a number of portraits of famous Edinburgh citizens and other Scots luminaries that had the tombs of Greyfriars Kirkyard as a backdrop.

It was in this kirkyard that a National Covenant, pledging defence of the Presbyterian religion, was signed in February of 1638.

Also a secretary to the Royal Scottish Academy (RSA), Hill died in 1870 and is buried in Edinburgh’s Dean Cemetery.

Scottish bearers of the Hill name have also thrived far from their native land as entrepreneurs, making a significant contribution to the nations in which they settled.

Not the least of these was John Hill, born in 1824 in Old Monklands, now part of Coatbridge, Lanarkshire.

Immigrating to the United States at the age of 20, he later settled in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, where his Scots-born uncle, Alexander Christie, owned a coalmine.

But, rather than entering his uncle’s business, he started an iron foundry in Baton Rouge and also operated a sawmill on the banks of the Mississippi and a ferry.

Marrying Catherine McPhail, originally from Glasgow, in 1851, the couple settled in a magnificent mansion in Baton Rouge’s Lafayette Street, while Hill also expanded his business interests by buying a sugar plantation.

It was the John Hill Foundry that built the imposing 1575ft. long cast-iron fence for the State of Louisiana’s state capitol building in Baton Rouge – a fence that was carefully repaired in 2009 in view of its historic importance.

His legacy also survives in the form of the Hill Memorial Library at Louisiana State University, founded by Hill, who died in 1910, in memory of his son, John Hill Jr.

Known as “The Empire Builder”, James Jerome Hill was the Canadian-American railroad tycoon who was born in 1838 in Eramosa Township, Ontario. Despite having had only nine years of formal education, he became chief executive of a number of railroad lines that came under the ‘umbrella’ of the Great Northern Railway.

This railroad empire, also known as the Hill Lines, covered a vast area that took in much of North America’s Upper Midwest, the Pacific Northwest and the northern Great Plains.

He died in 1916, and his heirs later established the James J. Hill Reference Library in St Paul, Minnesota.

Considered a premier source for publicly accessible business information in the United States, it now also boasts a number of online programmes that can be accessed by small business owners worldwide.

A great patron of the arts, one of Hill’s other legacies is his art collection now housed in the Minneapolis Institute of Arts.

On British shores, the mathematician Thomas Hill was part of a family dynasty of bearers of the name. Born in 1763 in Kidderminster, Worcestershire, he is credited with having invented the Single Transferable Vote (STV) system of proportional representation – first used in 1840 for election to Australia’s Adelaide City Council.

He died in 1851, and one of his sons was the British postal service reformer Sir Rowland Hill.

Born in 1795 in Kidderminster, it was through his appointment to reorganise the Post Office that he revolutionised the system by introducing the Uniform Penny Post and, in 1840, the adhesive postage stamp, which had been invented earlier.

Also a noted social reformer, he died in 1879 and is interred in Westminster Abbey.

There is a statue of him in London’s King Edward Street, while the Rowland Hill Awards, started in 1997 by the Royal Mail and the British Philatelic Trust, are awarded annually for philatelic innovation, initiative and enterprise.

His older brother, Edwin Hill, was also a postal reformer.

Born in 1793, he served, from 1840 to 1872, as the first British Controller of Stamps and was responsible in 1851 for the invention of the first mechanical system to make envelopes – the patent for which was later bought by Walter de la Rue.

Also a campaigner for Parliamentary reform, he died in 1876.

Renowned as Victorian-era social reformers, Miranda Hill and her sister Octavia were born in Wisbech, Cambridgeshire in, respectively, 1836 and 1838.

Octavia, concerned with the housing conditions of the urban poor, became a leading campaigner for the development of ‘social housing’ in suburban areas, while along with Miranda was instrumental in the foundation in 1876 of the Kyrle Society.

With the aim of “bringing art, books, music and open spaces into the lives of the urban poor”, the society is recognised as having provided the blueprint in 1896 for the foundation of the National Trust.

Miranda Hill died in 1910, while Octavia, who was also a member of the Royal Commission on Poor Laws, died two years later.

Those Normans who had fought on his behalf were rewarded with the lands of Anglo-Saxons, many of whom sought exile abroad as mercenaries.

name: Knight
history_english:
Ancient roots

A name of Anglo-Saxon origin, ‘Knight’ has been present in the British Isles from the earliest times.

Despite its strong martial and chivalric connotations, it derives from the Old English ‘cnicht’, which originally denoted either a serving lad or common soldier.

It was not until about the tenth century that it also came to denote a special military caste of fighting men, while following the Norman Conquest of 1066 ‘knighthood’ was recognised as one of the top ranks in feudal society.

Through time, ‘knighthood’ came to be bestowed not only in recognition of prowess on the battlefield but also as a social or civic distinction.

In the Peerage of the United Kingdom today, for example, the honour is bestowed for outstanding service in fields ranging from the arts and sciences to sport and business.

As a surname, ‘Knight’ stretches back through the dim mists of time, and flowing through the veins of many people of English birth today such as the Knights is the blood of those Germanic tribes who invaded and settled in the south and east of the island of Britain from about the early fifth century.

Known as the Anglo-Saxons, they were composed of the Jutes, from the area of the Jutland Peninsula in modern Denmark, the Saxons from Lower Saxony, in modern Germany and the Angles from the Angeln area of Germany.

It was the Angles who gave the name ‘Engla land’, or ‘Aengla land’ – better known as ‘England.’

They held sway in what became England from approximately 550 until the Conquest, with the main kingdoms those of Sussex, Wessex, Northumbria, Mercia, Kent, East Anglia and Essex.

The Knight name is first found in Suffolk before the Conquest, and figures prominently in the often turbulent historical record of England.

One noted late fifteenth and early sixteenth century bearer of the name was William Knight, the cleric, courtier and diplomat who served as Secretary of State to England’s Henry VIII.

Born in 1475 and educated at Winchester School and New College, Oxford, he first went to the royal court in 1495 as a secretary to Henry VIII’s predecessor, Henry VII.

Henry VIII succeeded to the throne in 1509 and, as one of his chaplains, Knight was present at the Field of the Cloth of Gold, near Calais, in 1520.

This was when Henry and Francis I of France staged a glittering tournament featuring their best knights in what proved to be an ultimately unsuccessful attempt to resolve their rival dynastic ambitions through a series of competitive martial contests.

Seven years later, Henry despatched Knight to Rome to plead with Pope Clement VII on his behalf to annul his marriage to his first wife, Catherine of Aragon, to allow him to marry Anne Boleyn.

Knight’s mission failed, but he was still held in high esteem by Henry; consecrated Bishop of Bath and Wells in 1541, he died in 1547.

Later in the sixteenth century, William Knight was the Roman Catholic martyr born in 1572 in South Duffield, Yorkshire.

An Anglican who secretly converted to the Catholic Church, he was aged 21 when he claimed from an uncle property which had been left to him by his father. It is doubtless for this reason that the uncle, unwilling to hand over property which was rightfully his nephew’s, denounced him to the authorities for being a Catholic.

This was at a time, during the reign of Queen Elizabeth I, when harsh Penal Laws were in place for those who practiced the outlawed Catholic faith.

Knight was confined to York Castle in October of 1593, where he languished for some time.

One of the other prisoners was a Church of England clergyman who had been arrested for participation in a rising in the north against the authorities.

In a bid to obtain his freedom and with the connivance of the authorities, he managed to convince Knight and two other Catholic prisoners, George Errington and William Gibson, that he wished to convert to Catholicism.

Winning their confidence and, again with the connivance of the authorities, he was released and made contact with a Henry Abbot of whom Knight, Errington and Gibson had spoken.

The unsuspecting Abbot attempted to procure a priest to arrange for the clergyman’s conversion, and was immediately arrested and thrown into prison.

Along with Knight, Errington and Gibson, he was accused of attempting to persuade a member of the Church of England to embrace Catholicism.

This was considered an act of treason under the Penal Laws and all four were executed through the barbaric ordeal of being hanged, drawn and quartered.

The four, along with 81 other Catholic martyrs of England and Wales, were beatified by Pope John Paul II in November of 1987 during his Papal Visit to the United Kingdom.

One intrepid bearer of the name was the English merchant and explorer James Knight, born in 1640.

Travelling to North America and joining the Hudson’s Bay Company in 1676 as a carpenter, just six years later he was appointed to the lucrative post of the company’s chief factor of the trading post of Fort Albany, in James Bay, at the southern end of Hudson Bay, Canada.

Later wealthy enough to buy stock in the company, he was appointed one of its directors.

During the 1702 to 1713 War of the Spanish Succession between England and France, a conflict that spread from the battlefields of Europe to North America, Fort Albany was captured by the French – but Knight led an armed expedition and recaptured it.

One of his obsessions was to find the elusive Northwest Passage – a route connecting the Atlantic and Pacific oceans through the Canadian North.

In 1719 he outfitted two ships – the Discovery and the Albany – to search for the route.

Despite being aged nearly 80, he embarked on one of the vessels, but both were wrecked off Marble Island, located within Western Hudson Bay.

Knight and other survivors of the shipwrecks established a small settlement on Marble Island and it is here that they all died from famine and sickness in about 1721.

It was not until 46 years later that the settlement was discovered by the Hudson’s Bay explorer Samuel Hearne.

Battle honours

On the high seas, Admiral Sir John Knight was a noted British Royal Navy officer during the American War of Independence of 1775 to 1783 and the French Revolutionary Wars of 1792 to 1802.

Born in 1747 in Dundee, Scotland, a son of Rear-Admiral John Knight, he served for a time during the American War of Independence aboard the sloop HMS Haerlem, conducting raiding operations along America’s Eastern Seaboard.

During the French Revolutionary Wars, he held commands that included the Barfleur in the Channel Fleet and HMS Victory in the Mediterranean; he died in 1831.

Also on the high seas, but in contemporary times, Roger John Beckett Knight, better known as R.J.B. Knight, is a leading British naval historian of the eighteenth century.

Born in 1944, and a former deputy director of the National Maritime Museum, Greenwich, he was appointed Visiting Professor of Naval History in the Greenwich Maritime Institute in 2001.

His acclaimed 2005 book The Pursuit of Victory: The Life and Achievement of Horatio Nelson, was the recipient of the Anderson Medal of the Society of Nautical Research, The Mountbatten Maritime Prize and the Duke of Westminster’s Medal for Military Literature.

From warfare at sea to warfare on land, Jack Knight was a posthumous recipient of the Medal of Honor, the United States military’s highest award for valour in the face of enemy action.

Born in Gamer, Texas, in 1917, he had been a first lieutenant in the 124th Cavalry Regiment when, in February of 1945 in Burma, he performed the actions for which he was awarded the honour.

Wounded after single-handedly destroying two Japanese pillboxes, he led his platoon in attacks on other enemy positions before being killed.

One particularly daring female bearer of the Knight name was Marguerite Diana Frances Knight, better known as Peggy Knight.

Born of mixed British and French parentage in Paris in 1920 but later settling in England before the outbreak of the Second World War in 1939, she found employment as a shorthand typist for an electrical company in Walthamstow, London.

It was early in 1944 that high-ranking members of the British intelligence organisation, the Special Operations Executive (SOE), by chance happened to hear her conversing in fluent French in a café.

Approached by SOE, the 24-year-old was immediately recruited and, after being rushed through a two-week training course, sent into France as a courier.

Using the codename “Nicole”, she worked for SOE’s “Donkeyman” network – relaying information between French Resistance and SOE.

Following the Allied invasion of Normandy in June of 1944, she criss-crossed the German and Allied lines carrying vital intelligence on enemy strengths and deployments.

With machine-gun in hand, she participated in a Resistance attack on a German convoy and later only narrowly escaped capture after her network was betrayed.

She died in 2004, the recipient of honours that include the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire, the French Croix de Guerre and America’s Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Born in 1877 in Long Eaton, Derbyshire, Laura Knight, more properly known as Dame Laura Knight, served as a British war artist during the Second World War, working on a number of commissions for the War Artists Advisory Committee at the Ministry of Information.

Works from this period include her 1942 A Balloon Site, Coventry and her 1944 Take Off, while she was also the official artist at the Nuremberg Trials of Nazi war criminals.

Born Laura Johnston, she had married fellow artist Harold Knight in 1903 and the couple settled in an artists’ colony in Newlyn, Cornwall.

In addition to her work as a war artist, she is also known for her Impressionist paintings of London’s colourful world of theatre and ballet.

Made Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE) in 1929, mainly in recognition of her Impressionist work, in 1936 she became the first woman elected to the prestigious Royal Academy; she died in 1970 at the age of 93.

Going much further back in time and to the world of social activism and politics, Anne Knight was an English pioneer of feminism and social reform.

Born into a Quaker family in Chelmsford, Essex, in 1786, she founded a local branch of the Women’s Anti-Slavery Society.

But when women were barred from participating in the 1840 World Anti-Slavery Convention in London, she was so incensed that she started to campaign for women’s rights.

The first leaflet arguing the case for women’s suffrage was produced by her in 1847 while four years later, along with Anne Kent, she formed the Sheffield Female Political Association – the first British organisation to campaign for women to be given the vote.

She died in 1862, while her birthplace in Chelmsford, now a Grade II listed building and used for a time as a Quaker Meeting House, is named Anne Knight Building in her honour.

Bearers of the name of Knight have also made their mark in the world of publishing.

Born in Windsor in about 1799, Charles Knight was the English publisher, editor and author who, after working as a journalist, founded Knight’s Quarterly Magazine in 1823.

Later superintendent of the publications for the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge, in 1828 he started the annual British Almanack and Companion.

As a publisher in his own right, he also founded The Library of Entertaining Knowledge and, in the early 1830s, the highly popular Penny Magazine and Penny Cyclopedia.

Also credited as the inventor in 1834 of stamped newspaper wrappers, he died in 1873.

Across the Atlantic, Charles Landon Knight, better known as C.L. Knight, was the American lawyer, politician and newspaper publisher who laid the foundation for what would become after his death today’s Knight Ridder group of newspapers.

Born in 1867 near Milledgeville, Georgia, he practised as a lawyer for a time before representing Ohio from 1921 to 1923 in the House of Representatives.

Earlier, in 1903, he had bought the Akron Beacon Journal, in Akron, Ohio.

On his death in 1933, the newspaper passed to his eldest son, John Shively Knight, born in 1894.

Better known as J.S. Knight, it was along with his brother James Landon Knight, born in 1909 and better known as James L. Knight, that he expanded his newspaper interests.

Purchasing the Miami Herald in 1937, by 1974 he and his brother owned fifteen newspapers across the United States, and it was in that year they merged their company with Ridder Publications to form Knight Ridder group of newspapers.

John S. Knight, the recipient of the 1968 Pulitzer Prize for editorial writing, died in 1981, while his brother died ten years later.

Before their deaths, they had founded the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation dedicated to the promotion of journalistic causes.

Ranked at the time of writing as the 47th richest person in the world and the 19th richest person in the United States, Philip Hampson Knight, better known as Phil Knight, is the entrepreneur who co-founded the global Nike brand of sportswear – in particular its range of running shoes.

Born in 1938 in Oregon, the son of a newspaper publisher, he worked in a number of jobs, including accountancy before, in 1969, along with Bill Bowerman, founding what became Nike – named after the Greek winged goddess of victory.

name: Matthews
history_english:
Celtic pedigree

Derived from the popular personal name ‘Matthew’, the surname ‘Matthews’, indicating ‘son of Matthew’, is of ancient Hebrew roots.

Meaning ‘gift of Jehovah’, or ‘gift of God’, it derives from the Hebrew personal name ‘Mattathaigh’, whose Latinised forms are ‘Matheus’ and ‘Mattheus’.

Ranked at 95th in some lists of the 100 most common surnames in England, it is nevertheless particularly identified with Wales.

Although, in common with many other surnames, it was popularised in the wake of the Norman Conquest of 1066, some of those who would later adopt the name pre-date the arrival on British shores of invaders such as the Romans, Vikings, Anglo-Saxons and Normans.

This means that flowing through the veins of many bearers of the Matthews name today is the blood of the ancient Britons.

Of Celtic pedigree, these early inhabitants of the British Isles were settled for centuries from a line south of the River Forth in Scotland all the way down to the south coast of England and with a particular presence in Wales.

Speaking a Celtic language known as Brythonic, they boasted a glorious culture that flourished even after the Roman invasion of Britain in 43 AD and the subsequent consolidation of Roman power by about 84 AD.

With many of the original Britons absorbing aspects of Roman culture, they became ‘Romano-British’ – while still retaining their own proud Celtic heritage.

Following the withdrawal of the last Roman legions from Britain in 406, what is now modern-day Wales, or Cymru, fragmented into a number of independent kingdoms – with the most powerful king being recognised as overall ruler.

Recognised as King of the Britons, he had to battle with not only internal rivals but also the depredations of the wild sea rovers known as the Vikings, or Northmen.

There were also the Anglo-Saxons to contend with – as those Germanic tribes who invaded and settled in the south and east of the island of Britain from about the early fifth century were known.

These Anglo-Saxons were composed of the Jutes, from the area of the Jutland Peninsula in modern Denmark, the Saxons from Lower Saxony, in modern Germany and the Angles from the Angeln area of Germany.

It was the Angles who gave the name ‘Engla land’, or ‘Aengla land’ – better known as ‘England.’

The Anglo-Saxons held sway in what became England from approximately 550 to 1066, with the main kingdoms those of Sussex, Wessex, Northumbria, Mercia, Kent, East Anglia and Essex.

Whoever controlled the most powerful of these kingdoms was tacitly recognised as overall ‘king’ – one of the most noted being Alfred the Great, King of Wessex from 871 to 899.

The Anglo-Saxons, meanwhile, had usurped the power of the indigenous Britons, such as those found in Wales, and who referred to them as ‘Saeson’ or ‘Saxones.’

It is from this that the Scottish Gaelic term for ‘English people’ of ‘Sasannach’ derives, the Irish Gaelic ‘Sasanach’ and the Welsh ‘Saeson.’

The death knell of Anglo-Saxon supremacy and also what remained of Welsh independence was sounded with the Norman Conquest and the defeat of Harold II, the last of the Anglo-Saxon monarchs, at the battle of Hastings.

Within an astonishingly short space of time, Norman manners, customs and law were imposed on England – laying the basis for what subsequently became established ‘English’ custom and practice.

In 1282, by which time most of Wales had come under Anglo-Norman rule, final rebellion against this was crushed by England’s Edward I, and it is from this date that the heir apparent to the British throne has borne the title of Prince of Wales.

An abortive rebellion was led in the early fifteenth century by the freedom fighter Owain Glyndŵr, while in the following century, under Henry VIII, Wales was ‘incorporated’ into the English kingdom; in 1707, in common with Scotland, Wales became part of the United Kingdom.

Flourishing not only in their original heartland of Wales but also throughout the British Isles, bearers of the Matthews name feature prominently in the historical record.

Born in 1826 into a prominent Herefordshire family, Henry Matthews, 1st Viscount Llandaff, was the lawyer and Conservative Party politician known for his role in a sensational late nineteenth century divorce case that led to the ruin of a prominent Liberal Party politician. It was a case that rocked the establishment and one that today would give rise to lurid tabloid newspaper headlines.

Called to the bar in 1850 after being educated in both London and Paris, Matthews was made a Queen’s Counsel in 1868.

He quickly gained a formidable reputation for his incisive examination of witnesses – a talent that was put to the test with great success in the 1885 court case involving Sir Charles Wentworth Dilke, 2nd Baronet.

Born in 1843, the Liberal politician had been elected Member of Parliament (MP) for Chelsea in 1868 and served as Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs from 1880 to 1882, was admitted to the Privy Council in 1882 and, in the same year, appointed to the Cabinet as President of the Local Government Board.

His second marriage was to the art historian, feminist and trade unionist Emilia, Lady Dilke, while his younger brother Ashton Wentworth Dilke was married to Mary Eustace Smith, the eldest daughter of the Liberal politician and ship-owner Thomas Eustace Smith and his wife Ellen.

In a highly complex tale of adultery and infidelity, Sir Charles Dilke had begun an affair with Ellen Smith in 1884, the same year as his marriage to the unsuspecting Emilia.

The seeds of his spectacular fall from grace were sown in July of 1885 when his lover’s youngest daughter, Virginia, claimed he had seduced her.

She claimed this had first occurred when she was aged 19, in 1882, and shortly after her marriage to the MP Donald Crawford. The affair is said to have continued for about two and a half years.

Crawford sued for divorce from Virginia in February of 1886 and the case was brought before the Honourable Mr Justice Butt.

Virginia Crawford did not appear in court, while Dilke refused to give evidence – and the judge subsequently delivered the rather bizarre judgement that while Virginia had been guilty of adultery with Dilke, there was no admissible evidence that he had been guilty of adultery with her.

Granting a decree nisi, dissolving the Crawford marriage, he also said he could see no case whatsoever against Dilke and dismissed him from the suit with costs.

But an investigative journalist, William Stead, launched a public campaign against Dilke who, in a bid to clear his name sought to reopen the whole sordid case.

This was to prove his downfall.

In the subsequent trial he was subjected to a gruelling cross-examination by Henry Matthews, acting on behalf of Crawford, and the jury found that Virginia Crawford had indeed been telling the truth that she had been seduced by Dilke.

Evidence elicited by Matthews that proved particularly incriminating was that Dilke had physically cut out evidence of potentially embarrassing facts from his diaries.

Dilke, his reputation in tatters, was ruined and lost his Parliamentary seat shortly afterwards.

It was on the strength of his performance at the trial that, as Conservative MP for Birmingham East, Matthews was appointed Home Secretary in the Cabinet of Lord Salisbury – some sources asserting this had been at the insistence of Queen Victoria who had been impressed by him.

As Home Secretary, he served in the post during the gruesome ‘Jack the Ripper’ Whitechapel murders of 1881 to 1891; ennobled as Viscount Llandaff in 1895, he died eight years later.

Science and invention

From politics and the law to the worlds of the sciences and invention, bearers of the Matthews name have also stamped a significant mark on the historical record.

A British marine geologist and geophysicist, Drummond Hoyle Matthews was a pioneering contributor to the theory of plate tectonics – involving variations in the properties of rocks forming on the ocean floor leading to what is known as ‘seafloor spreading.’

Born in 1931 his work, along with that of fellow British geologist and geophysicist Fred Vine and the Canadian Lawrence Morley, is recognised as having played a crucial role in the development and acceptance by the scientific community of the theory of plate tectonics.

A research fellow at King’s College, Cambridge and the recipient of the Geological Society of London’s prestigious Wollaston Medal, he died in 1997.

Born in India in 1919, Paul Matthews was the British theoretical physicist who headed the physics department of Imperial College, London and served for a time as chairman of the Nuclear Physics Board of the Science Research Council.

Also vice-chancellor of the University of Bath and a Fellow of the Royal Society and a recipient of the Rutherford Medal, he died in 1987.

Born in 1936 in Tulsa, Oklahoma, Gordon Matthews was the American inventor and businessman who founded the company that pioneered the commercialisation of voicemail.

Although it was first invented in 1976 by Stephen Boies of IBM, it was Matthews who three years later became the first to exploit it commercially.

Joining the U.S. Marine Corps as a pilot after graduating from the University of Tulsa in 1959, Matthews was first drawn to the challenge of attempting to ‘mesh’ human voices to technology after a fellow pilot was killed in a mid-air collision.

The accident, Matthews believed, had been caused by the pilot having to briefly take his eyes of the aircraft’s controls in order to adjust his radio frequency.

Working for IBM, he helped to develop voice-activated cockpit controls and, after a period with Texas Instruments founded his own company ECS Communications in 1979.

Partly based on Stephen Boies’ original invention, Matthews submitted a patent for ‘Voice Message Exchange’, or voicemail, subsequently refining the technique with a further 35 patents.

Later changing the name of his company to VMX Inc., the first company to sell voicemail technology for corporate use, he died in 2002.

One particularly colourful and enigmatic bearer of the Matthews name was the British inventor Harry Grindell Matthews, who claimed to have invented that ultimate weapon of war – the death ray.

Born in 1880 in Winterbourne, Gloucestershire, he served during the Second Boer War of 1899 to 1902 with the South African Constabulary and was wounded twice.

Back in Britain, he claimed in 1911 to have invented an ‘aerophone’ device capable of transmitting messages between a ground station and an aeroplane from a distance of two miles.

Intrigued by this, the British War Office requested a demonstration – but Matthews demanded that no ‘experts’ be present and, when the observers began taking notes, he rapidly dismantled his equipment and declared the ‘demonstration’ to be at an end.

Although the War Office declared the demonstration to have been a complete failure, the colourfully extrovert Matthews proved popular with the Press, who rushed to his defence.

Shortly after the outbreak of the First World War in 1914, the War Office offered an award of £25,000 to anyone who could create a weapon capable of dealing with Germany’s feared motorised air balloons known as Zeppelins.

First to rise to the challenge was the bold Matthews, who managed to demonstrate a remote controlled device, using selenium cells, against a remotely controlled boat in the Penn Pond in London’s Richmond Park.

He was awarded the £25,000 but, for reasons that remain unclear, the War Office never took up the idea.

The inventor was in the public eye again in 1923 when he claimed to have invented a ‘death ray’ that could not only kill humans but also put electrical devices out of action.

He apparently demonstrated this to an overawed journalist by stopping a motorcycle engine from a distance.

Newspapers rushed into print with sensational accounts of the death ray, and in February of 1944 the War Office requested a demonstration.

In one such demonstration he did indeed successfully use a ‘ray’ to switch on a light bulb and cut off a motor, but the War Office remained unconvinced.

Matthews haughtily refused to give further demonstrations and instead threatened to sell his deadly invention to a foreign power.

Some inducements were offered for him not to do so, but he attempted to tout the idea to both France and the USA – until they, exasperated by his failure to provide convincing proof of his invention, in common with the War Office lost all interest.

Nevertheless still a magnet for wealthy private investors for other inventions that included the Sky Projector, capable of projecting pictures onto clouds, he was able to build a laboratory and private airfield at Tor Clawdd, in Betws, South Wales, where he had settled.

Later marrying the immensely wealthy Polish-American opera singer and perfumist Ganna Walska, he died in 1941.

From science and invention to the highly competitive world of business, Sir Terence Matthews is the leading Welsh-Canadian hi-tech entrepreneur and business magnate born in 1943 in Newport, South Wales and Wales’s first billionaire.

Immigrating to Canada as a young man after obtaining a degree in electronics from Swansea University, he still retains strong connections to the land of his birth.

With interests in a number of international companies that include Newbridge Networks and Mitel, of which he is chairman at the time of writing, he is also the owner of the Celtic Manor Resort Complex in Newport, near the South Wales coast, and which was host to golf’s 2012 Ryder Cup.

The Celtic Manor Hotel, meanwhile, is the former maternity hospital where he was born; knighted in 2001, he is also the recipient of an OBE.

A multi-millionaire with a fortune estimated at £300m at the time of his death in 2010, Bernard Matthews was the British businessman who was a popular household name for many years.

Born in 1930 in Brooke, Norfolk, the son of a car mechanic, it was in 1950 that he founded Bernard Matthews Farms Ltd., the Norfolk-based company known for farming turkey and producing turkey products.

The company launched its first television commercial, for Turkey Breast Roast, in 1980, and Matthews became famous for his catchphrase “Bootiful”, delivered in a strong Norfolk accent, to describe the product.

Also known for his philanthropy and the recipient of a CBE, he was appointed a Commander of the Royal Victorian Order (CVO) four years before his death for his services to the Duke of Edinburgh’s Award Scheme.

name: Percy
history_english:
On the field of battle

A name that resonates throughout the pages of the high drama that is England’s frequently turbulent historical record, ‘Percy’ is particularly noted as the family name of the Dukes of Northumberland, and the history of the Percys is in effect that of the famed House of Percy.

Deriving from the original family baronial manor of Percy-en-Auge, Normandy, it stems from the Gallo-Roman personal name ‘Persius’, while its Latin version is ‘Persiacum’ and Old French form ‘Perci.’

It first arrived on English shores in the wake of Duke William of Normandy’s Conquest of 1066, a pivotal event in the nation’s history.

By this date, England had become a nation with several powerful competitors to the throne.

In what were extremely complex family, political and military machinations, the English monarch was Harold II, who had succeeded to the throne following the death of Edward the Confessor.

But his right to the throne was contested by two powerful competitors – his brother-in-law King Harold Hardrada of Norway, in alliance with Tostig, Harold II’s brother, and Duke William II of Normandy.

In what has become known as The Year of Three Battles, Hardrada invaded England and gained victory over the English king on September 20 at the battle of Fulford, in Yorkshire.

Five days later, however, Harold decisively defeated his brother-in-law and brother at the battle of Stamford Bridge.

But he had little time to celebrate his victory, having to immediately march south from Yorkshire to encounter a mighty invasion force, led by Duke William, that had landed at Hastings, in East Sussex.

Harold’s battle-hardened but exhausted force of Anglo-Saxon soldiers confronted the Normans on October 14, drawing up a strong defensive position at the top of Senlac Hill and building a shield wall to repel their cavalry and infantry.

The Normans suffered heavy losses, but through a combination of the deadly skill of their archers and the ferocious determination of their cavalry they eventually won the day.

Anglo-Saxon morale had collapsed on the battlefield as word spread through the ranks that Harold, the last of the Anglo-Saxon kings, had been killed.

William was declared King of England on December 25, and the complete subjugation of his Anglo-Saxon subjects followed, with those Normans who had supported him rewarded with their lands.

Within an astonishingly short space of time, Norman manners, customs and law were imposed on England – laying the basis for what subsequently became established ‘English’ custom and practice.

The roots of what became the mighty House of Percy – through time boasting titles that include Baron Percy, Earl of Egremont, Earl of Northumberland, Earl of Worcester and Duke of Northumberland – can be traced back to a year after the conquest when William de Percy crossed from his native Normandy to England to lend further support to William in the consolidation of his power.

Created 1st Baron of Topcliffe, in Yorkshire, he was the progenitor of a number of illustrious bearers of the name who feature prominently in the historical record.

He died in 1096, while one of his descendants was Sir Richard de Percy, 5th Baron Percy.

Born in about 1170, he was the son of Agnes de Perci – who became heiress of the Percy estates after the name died out in the male line – and Joscelin of Louvain, who assumed the Percy surname after his marriage to Agnes.

Sir Richard de Percy was one of the English magnates who participated in the First Barons’ War against the highly unpopular rule of the Plantagenet King John.

This war culminated in the king being forced in June of 1215, at Runnymede, to append his seal to the charter of English liberties known as the Magna Carta, or Great Charter, and which held that no-one was above the laws of the realm, including the monarch.

Sir Richard was one of 25 barons charged with attempting to enforce the king’s adherence to the charter, but war broke out again and he, along with his nephew William de Percy, had his lands declared forfeit after rising again in rebellion.

But his estates were restored after the death of King John in 1216, and the succession to the throne of Henry III.

Sir Richard died in 1244, while one of his descendants was Henry de Percy, born in 1273 and the son of Henry de Percy, 8th Baron Percy of Topcliffe, and Eleanor de Warrene, daughter of John de Warrene, Earl of Surrey.

Fighting under Edward I in his subjugation of both Wales and Scotland, he was present at the battle of Falkirk in July of 1298 when the army of the great Scottish freedom fighter William Wallace was routed.

Granted estates in Scotland – later retaken by the Scottish warrior king Robert the Bruce – it was in 1309 that he purchased from Anthony Bek, Prince Bishop of Durham, the barony of Alnwick and the fortress of Alnwick Castle, in Northumberland.

Guarding a road crossing the River Aln, the first parts of the castle had been constructed about thirty years after the Norman Conquest by Yves de Vesacy, Baron of Alnwick, in order to protect England’s northern border with Scotland from invasion and also from the notorious border reivers.

These reivers took their name from their lawless custom of reiving, or raiding, not only their neighbours’ livestock, but also that of their English counterparts.

The word ‘bereaved’, for example, indicating to have suffered loss, derives from the original ‘reived’, meaning to have suffered loss of property.

A constant thorn in the flesh of both the English and Scottish authorities was the cross-border raiding and pillaging carried out by these well-mounted and heavily armed men, the contingent from the Scottish side of the border known and feared as ‘moss troopers.’

In an attempt to bring order to what was known as the wild ‘debateable land’ on both sides of the border, Alexander II of Scotland had in 1237 signed the Treaty of York, which for the first time established the Scottish border with England as a line running from the Solway to the Tweed.

On either side of the border there were three ‘marches’ or areas of administration, the West, East, and Middle Marches, and a warden governed these.

Complaints from either side of the border were dealt with on Truce days, when the wardens of the different marches would act as arbitrators. There was also a law known as the Hot Trod, that granted anyone who had their livestock stolen the right to pursue the thieves and recover their property.

It was after taking possession of Alnwick Castle that Henry Percy began a major programme of rebuilding the forbidding edifice, with work continuing following his death in 1314 under his son Henry de Percy.

Knightly prowess

Born in 1299, Henry de Percy, in common with his father, became embroiled in the interminable and exhausting warfare with Scotland.

Present at the battle of Halidon Hill in 1333, he was also placed in command of the right wing of the English army at the 1346 battle of Neville’s Cross.

He died in 1352, while his son, also Henry, 3rd Baron Percy of Alnwick, participated in the 1356 invasion of his northern neighbour that saw the humiliation of Edward Balliol’s surrender of the Scottish kingdom and his crown to Edward III.

His son, Henry Percy, 1st Earl of Northumberland and 4th Baron Percy, was one of the many victims of the complex political manoeuvrings and swiftly changing loyalties of his time.

Appointed at the age of only 21 to the powerful and trusted post of Warden of the Marches – giving him authority to negotiate on the English king’s behalf with Scotland – he was created 1st Earl of Northumberland under Richard II and, under Henry IV, given the lordship of the Isle of Man and appointed Constable of England.

But in 1403, for a number of reasons that included incurring the king’s wrath for attempting to resolve the rebellion against English rule that raged in Wales by seeking an accommodation with the rebels he, along with his eldest son Sir Henry Percy, better known to posterity as Sir Harry Hotspur, rebelled against Henry in favour of Edward Mortimer, 5th Earl of March.

The rebellion was crushed at the battle of Shrewsbury in July of 1403, and Hotspur was among the slain.

Another rebellion followed two years later and, after it was also quashed, Percy was forced to flee to Scotland. With Scottish support, he invaded his homeland in 1408, but was killed at the battle of Bramham Moor.

Sir Harry Hotspur, meanwhile, born at the family seat of Alnwick Castle in 1364, was renowned as one of the most valiant knights in Christendom.

Knighted when aged only 13 by Edward III, he soon stamped a memorable mark on the turbulent times in which he lived.

By 1380 he was campaigning in Ireland, travelling two years later to Prussia.

Appointed Warden of the East March in 1384, he was at the side of Richard II a year later on an expedition over the border into hostile Scotland – the Scots, who grudgingly admired his knightly prowess, giving him the nickname of ‘Haatspore’, ‘Hotspur’, in recognition of his lightning speed while on campaign and readiness to attack and fall on the enemy.

He also campaigned on behalf of his king in France, leading devastating raids into Picardy, while in 1388 he was back in Scotland in command of the English forces at the battle of Otterburn in August of that year.

A Scots army commanded by the earls of Douglas, Moray and Mar had invaded the northern reaches of Northumberland a few weeks earlier and Hotspur was in command of an English force despatched to meet them at Newcastle.

Vicious hand-to-hand fighting ensued, and the Earl of Douglas is reputed to have captured Hotspur’s pennant – the equivalent of an army regiment losing its proud Colours to the enemy – and boasted he would affix it to the walls of his stronghold at Dalkeith.

The Scots retreated about one mile northwest of Otterburn, and it was here that a fierce battle was joined on August 5. The Scots proved victorious – although the Earl of Douglas was slain – and Hotspur captured; it was only after payment of a hefty ransom that he was released from captivity.

Both he and Douglas subsequently became the heroes of the famous The Ballad of Chevy Chase.

Along with his father, Hotspur also fought at the battle of Homildon Hill in September of 1402, where the Scottish commander Archibald Douglas, 4th Earl of Douglas, was taken prisoner.

On a particularly macabre note, following his death at the battle of Shrewsbury, Hotspur’s body was later exhumed from its grave on the orders of the king after wild rumours began to circulate that he had not been killed.

His head was impaled on one of the city gates of York, while his body was quartered and sent to Newcastle upon Tyne, London, Bristol and Chester. His remains were later returned to his widow and interred in York Minster – while it is as ‘Hotspur’ that he is memorably portrayed in Shakespeare’s play Henry IV, Part I.

The 18th century guard tower at Alnwick is named Hotspur’s Seat, while the castle’s Constable Tower is host to a special Harry Hotspur exhibition.

In contemporary times, the bold Hotspur also gives his name to Tottenham Hotspur Football Club – because the Percy family once owned a family seat in the area.

Through his marriage to Elizabeth Mortimer, eldest daughter of Edmund Mortimer, 3rd Earl of March, Hotspur had two children – Elizabeth Percy and Henry Percy, 2nd Earl of Northumberland, born in 1393.

This second earl was an early victim of the 1455 to 1487 conflict between the House of York and the House of Lancaster – known as the Wars of the Roses – for possession of the English Crown.

It was while fighting on the Lancastrian side that he was killed in May of 1455 at the first battle of St Albans.

Through his marriage to Eleanor Neville, daughter of Henry V’s aunt Joan Beaufort, Countess of Westmorland, he was the father of ten children.

One of them, Henry Percy, 3rd Earl of Northumberland, was killed at the battle of Towton in March of 1461, while Thomas Percy, 1st Baron Egremont, was killed at the battle of Northampton in 1460.

In April of 1463, yet another Percy, Sir Ralph, fell while fighting for the Lancastrian cause in the battle of Hedgeley Moor.

Amidst the shifting loyalties of the time, Henry Percy, 4th Earl of Northumberland, fought on the Yorkist side, commanding the reserve at the battle of Bosworth Field in August of 1485.

He survived the battle – only to meet a gruesome end four years later when he was lynched by rioting citizens of York in what was known as the Yorkshire Rebellion over high taxation.

Born in 1477, Henry Algernon Percy, 5th Earl of Northumberland, was an influential member of the courts of both Henry VII and his successor Henry VIII and also for a time an army commander.

He died in 1527, while his son Henry Percy, born in 1502 and 6th Earl of Northumberland, is best remembered for having had to break his betrothal to the ill-fated Anne Boleyn, after she came to the lascivious attention of Henry VIII.

Sir Thomas Percy, born in 1504, was subjected to the brutal ordeal of being hanged, drawn and quartered in Tyburn, London, in June of 1537 after being convicted of treason.

This was for his role in what was known as the Pilgrimage of Grace, the rising that broke out in Yorkshire in the autumn of 1536 in protest against Henry VIII’s decisive break with the Roman Catholic Church and his subsequent dissolution of the monasteries.

Another martyr to the Catholic faith was his son, Thomas Percy, who was executed for treason at York in August of 1572 for his part in the Rising of the North. He was later beatified by the Catholic Church as Blessed Thomas Percy.

His brother, Henry Percy, 8th Earl of Northumberland, had remained loyal to Queen Elizabeth I during the Rising, but later fell victim to his alleged role in a plot to free the deposed Mary, Queen of Scots, from her captivity in England.

Confined to the Tower of London, he was found dead in his cell in June of 1585, having been shot through the heart.

A verdict of suicide was hastily recorded – but conspiracy theories still exist as to whether or not he had indeed taken his own life.

One of his sons, George Percy, born in 1580 and who died in 1632, was an early governor of Virginia, while another son, Henry Percy, 9th Earl of Northumberland, became better known as “The Wizard Earl.”

This was a sobriquet he acquired through his wide-ranging scientific interests and experiments that included the mysterious art of alchemy – attempting to turn base metals into gold – and cartography.

Born in 1564, he is recognised as having been one of the wealthiest noblemen in the court of Elizabeth I and, along with his distant relation Thomas Percy, was implicated in the abortive Gunpowder Plot of November 1605 against her successor James I (James VI of Scotland).

This was an attempt by dissident English Catholic gentry to blow up the king, the Lords and the Commons at the formal opening of Parliament.

The Wizard Earl was confined for a time in the Tower of London before being allowed to return to his estates, while Thomas Percy, along with the conspirator Robert Catesby, was shot dead while trying to evade capture.

The earl died in 1632, and through his marriage to Dorothy Devereux, a sister of Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex, he had four children.

Through one of these children, his eldest daughter Lady Dorothy Percy, who married Robert Sidney, 2nd Earl of Leicester, he was an ancestor of the late Diana, Princess of Wales.

name: Barnes
history_english:
Martyrs and poets

A name with several possible points of origin, ‘Barnes’ has been present throughout the British Isles from earliest times and is particularly prevalent in England.

As a locational surname, it is thought to have derived from the parish of Barnes, in Surrey, while as an occupation name it may derive from someone who worked in a barn.

As a topographical surname, it may have referred to someone who lived near a barn.

Some sources assert the name is of ancient Anglo-Saxon roots, derived from the Old English ‘beorn’, indicating ‘warrior’, while other sources claim it was first introduced to England in the wake of the mid-eleventh century Norman Conquest in the form of the French ‘de Barnes’ or ‘le Barne.’

A distinguished family of the name was indeed granted lands in Cambridgeshire as reward for their assistance in 1066 to William of Normandy at the battle of Hastings.

This does not preclude the fact that there may have already been Anglo-Saxons of the name present in England.

These Anglo-Saxons stemmed from those Germanic tribes who invaded and settled in the south and east of the island of Britain from about the early fifth century.

Composed of the Jutes, from the area of the Jutland Peninsula in modern Denmark, the Saxons from Lower Saxony, in modern Germany and the Angles from the Angeln area of Germany, they held sway in what became England from approximately 550 to 1066.

It was the Angles who gave the name ‘Engla land’, or ‘Aengla land’ – better known as ‘England.’

Yet another theory of the origin of the Barnes name is that it stems from the Middle English and the Scottish ‘bairn’, indicating a small child.

Bearers of the Barnes name feature prominently in England’s historical record – no less so than Robert Barnes, also known as Robert Barnes the Martyr.

Born in 1495 in Lynn, Suffolk, he is considered to have preached the first sermon of what later became the tumultuous upheaval in religion known as the English Reformation.

Graduating with a degree in divinity from Cambridge University in 1523, he became prior of the university’s religious order of the Austin Friars.

It was at the Christmas midnight mass of 1525 that Barnes preached a fiery sermon accusing the established Church of heresy – a sermon that sent shock waves through the religious community and is seen as the first such attack on the Roman Catholic Church in England.

Brought before prominent churchmen who included Cardinal Wolsey, he in turn was accused of heresy and given the stark options of either recanting his sermon or being burned at the stake.

Barnes reluctantly recanted and, after being imprisoned for a time, fled to Antwerp where he made the acquaintance of other religious reformers who included Martin Luther.

Returning to England in 1531, he was enlisted by Henry VIII to petition the Pope on his behalf for his divorce from Catherine of Aragon and, four years later, he was again employed on the English monarch’s behalf in the negotiations to settle his marriage to Anne of Cleves.

As religious discontent swelled and the divide deepened between the Roman Catholic Church and the ‘Protesters’, better known as ‘Protestants’, he was burned at the stake in July of 1540 along with five others after preaching yet another sermon attacking the Church.

In later decades, one particularly volatile bearer of the Barnes name was the English poet Barnabe Barnes, born in York in 1571.

The third son of Dr Richard Barnes, Bishop of Durham, he became famous for his love sonnets and infamous for his explosive temperament.

He became embroiled in 1598 in what were known as the ‘pamphlet wars’ among the literati of the day over what constituted ‘good’ poetry.

Barnes took exception to the comments of one pamphleteer, John Browne, and ended by being put on trial for attempting to murder him on two occasions.

This was by offering him a poisoned lemon and then by sweetening his wine with sugar laced with mercury sublimate.

Browne survived the attempts on his life, while Barnes managed to escape while his trial was in progress.

Powerful family connections meant he was not pursued, and he died eleven years later.

Also of a combative temperament – but only through the medium of the written word – was the journalist Thomas Barnes, born in London in 1785.

Appointed editor of The Times in 1817, a post he held until his death in 1841, it was during his tenure that the newspaper became known as The Thunderer – as it railed against perceived injustices of the day and Government incompetence.

In much quieter literary mode, William Barnes was the poet best known for his Poems of Rural Life in Dorset. Born in 1800, the son of a farmer, he died in 1886.

The proud name of Barnes also features prominently in the Peerage of the United Kingdom.

Born in 1848, the son of a wealthy Liverpool ship owner, John Gorell Barnes was called to the Bar in 1876 after studying law at Cambridge University and became a Queens Counsel twelve years later.

Serving as President of the Probate, Divorce and Admiralty Division of the High Court of Justice from 1905 to 1909 and as a member of the Privy Council, he was elevated to the Peerage as 1st Baron Gorell four years before his death in 1913.

He was succeeded by his eldest son, Major Henry Gorell Barnes, 2nd Baron Gorell.

Born in 1882, he was killed in action on the Western Front in 1917 while serving with the Royal Field Artillery.

His brother, Ronald Gorell, succeeded him as 3rd Baron Gorell.

Not only a lawyer but also a Liberal Party politician, poet, author and editor, he was born in 1884.

Admitted as a barrister to London’s Inner Temple in 1909, he later worked from 1911 to 1915 as a journalist for The Times.

Serving for part of the First World War with the Rifle Brigade, where he attained the rank of captain, he was awarded the Military Cross in 1917.

Taking his seat as a Liberal peer in the House of Lords following the death of his brother, he served from 1921 to 1922 as Under-Secretary of State for Air.

Editor of Cornhill magazine from 1933 to 1939 he was also, along with the crime novelist Agatha Christie, co-president of the Detection Club from 1956 until his death in 1963.

Fame and infamy

Although early bearers of the Barnes name were to be found in their heartland of the British Isles, waves of emigration over the centuries saw the name also become rooted in foreign parts such as North America, Australia and New Zealand.

Born in 1866 in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, John Mahlon Barnes, better known to his contemporaries as Mahlon, was the socialist political activist who was a leading light of the Socialist Labor Party of America from 1891 to 1899 and a founding member in 1901 of the breakaway Socialist Party of America.

Barnes, the son of a boot maker and who had worked as a cigar maker before taking up full-time political activism, also served after the end of the First World War as head of the National League for the Release of Political Prisoners – set up to obtain pardons for imprisoned conscientious objectors.

He died in 1934.

Returning to British shores, George Barnes was the Scottish politician who served as leader of what was then the fledgling Labour Party from February 1910 until the following year. Born in 1859 in Lochend, Dundee, he began work at the age of 11 in a jute mill managed by his father.

This was in Ponders End, Middlesex, to where the family had moved.

Later undergoing an apprenticeship in engineering and working for a time in a foundry in his native Dundee and with the company of Lucas and Airds in Fulham, London, he became general secretary of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers.

Entering politics, in 1906 he was elected Labour Member of Parliament (MP) for the Glasgow seat of Blackfriars and Hutchesontown – becoming one of the first Labour MPs to be elected in Scotland.

Following his tenure as leader of the Labour Party, he served in a number of government posts that included Minister of Pensions in the First World War coalition government under David Lloyd George.

Author of a number of works that include his autobiographical From Workshop to War Cabinet, he died in 1940.

On the battlefield, James Barnes was a Union Army general of the American Civil War of 1861 to 1865. Born in 1801 in Boston and commissioned at the outbreak of the conflict into the 18th Massachusetts Regiment, he saw action in key battles that include the Second Battle of Bull Run, Antietam and the 1863 Gettysburg.

A railroad civil engineer before the war, it was to this career that he returned – serving as a member of the government commission that supervised the building of the Union Pacific Railroad; he died in 1869.

One bearer of the Barnes name whose legacy can be seen to this day on the American landscape was the American architect Edward Larrabee Barnes.

Architect of many noted edifices that include the IBM Building in Manhattan and the Dallas Museum of Art, his awards include a Fellowship of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and the Gold Medal of the American Institute of Architects.

Born in Chicago in 1915 and a graduate of the Harvard School of Design, he died in 2004.

One particularly infamous bearer of the Barnes name was George Celino Barnes, better known to posterity as the American bootlegger and armed robber Machine Gun Kelly.

Born in 1895 in Memphis, Tennessee, it was during the American Prohibition era of the ban on the sale and consumption of alcohol that he came to the attention of law enforcement officers as a bootlegger.

This involved smuggling alcohol into the United States, while also throughout the 1920s and 1930s he engaged in a series of armed robberies.

His favoured weapon was the deadly Thomson submachine gun, while he also changed his name to ‘George K. Kelly’ in what proved to be a futile bid to protect his family and evade the clutches of the law.

Sentenced to three years imprisonment in 1928 for smuggling alcohol, he later married Katherine Thorne.

As his career in crime continued, submachine gun in hand, the enterprising Katherine cashed in on her husband’s infamy by selling the expended .45 calibre cartridges from the weapon.

Katherine, by this time known as Katherine Kelly, joined her husband and his gang in what became even bolder criminal activities.

This culminated in 1933 when Machine Gun Kelly and his gang kidnapped and held to ransom the wealth Charles F. Urschel, from Oklahoma, and his friend Walter J. Jarrett.

The pair were released unharmed, but only after a ransom of $200,000 dollars had been received.

Unfortunately for Machine Gun Kelly, however, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), in the form of its formidable director J. Edgar Hoover, were quickly on the case.

Utilising pioneering crime investigation techniques that included state of the art fingerprinting techniques, Kelly and his gang were tracked down in what became the first major case in which the FBI, dubbed ‘G-Men’, meaning ‘Government Men’, were involved.

Machine Gun Kelly, a.k.a. George Celino Barnes, was brought to trial along with his wife and gang in October of 1933 and sentenced to life imprisonment.

Katherine was released from prison in 1958, four years after the death of her husband in the notorious Alcatraz Prison.

So subdued and such a model prisoner had the once feared Machine Gun Kelly become in prison that fellow inmates had mockingly referred to him as ‘Pop Gun Kelly.’

One truly adventurous and pioneering bearer of the Barnes name was Florence “Pancho” Barnes, the early twentieth century aviatrix born Florence Leontine Lowe in Pasadena, California in 1901.

Her grandfather, Thaddeus C.S. Lowe, had taken to the skies by establishing the Union Army Balloon Corps, to spy on the Confederate Army enemy, during the American Civil War.

But his granddaughter rose to even greater heights.

It was in 1919 that she married the Rev. C. Rankin Barnes and, nine years later, with the encouragement of a cousin, learned to fly.

Taking to the skies as if this was her natural habitat, in 1930 she broke Amelia Earhart’s world women’s speed record with a speed of 196.19mph (315.7km/h).

Much in demand as a highly skilled and daring lady of the skies, she became a stunt pilot – most notably performing dangerous stunts in the 1930 film Hell’s Angels.

She bought 180 acres of land in the Mojave Desert in 1935 and established what became the famous Happy Bottom Riding Club – also colourfully known as the Rancho Oro Verde Fly-Inn Dude Ranch – catering to pilots from the nearby U.S. Army airbase of March Field.

She died in 1975, while her daring life and times are portrayed in the 1983 film The Right Stuff, based on the book of the same name by Tom Wolfe.

name: May
history_english:
Ancient roots

A name with a number of points of origin, ‘May’ has been present in the British Isles from the earliest times.

In common with many other English surnames found today, it first came into popular vogue in the wake of the Norman Conquest of 1066 – but those who would later formally adopt the name had been present for a considerable period before this.

A name with what are known as ‘cognates’, or ‘versions’ in a number of European languages – such as the Germanic, or Anglo-Saxon, ‘Meir’ and ‘Meier’ – it originally denoted someone born, or baptised, in the verdant month of May.

Some sources, meanwhile, also state it may have once served as a nickname for someone noted for possessing a sunny temperament or disposition.

In addition to Anglo-Saxon roots, the name also has ancient Irish and Scots Gaelic roots – explaining why some bearers of the name today are recognised as a sept, or sub-branch, of the proud Scottish Clan Donald, while another derivation is from the Old French ‘mai’, in turn derived from the Latin ‘maius.’

All these sources of origin mean that flowing through the veins of many bearers of the name today is a rich and heady mix of the blood of not only Gaels but, particularly for those of English roots, the blood of Anglo-Saxons and Normans.

This provides for a colourful heritage infused with the vibrant drama that is England’s frequently turbulent history.

The ancient bloodline of the Mays includes that of this those Germanic tribes who invaded and settled in the south and east of the island of Britain from about the early fifth century.

Known as the Anglo-Saxons, they were composed of the Jutes, from the area of the Jutland Peninsula in modern Denmark, the Saxons from Lower Saxony, in modern Germany and the Angles from the Angeln area of Germany.

It was the Angles who gave the name ‘Engla land’, or ‘Aengla land’ – better known as ‘England.’

They held sway in what became England from approximately 550 to 1066, with the main kingdoms those of Sussex, Wessex, Northumbria, Mercia, Kent, East Anglia and Essex.

Whoever controlled the most powerful of these kingdoms was tacitly recognised as overall ‘king’ – one of the most noted being Alfred the Great, King of Wessex from 871 to 899.

It was during his reign that the famous Anglo-Saxon Chronicle was compiled – an invaluable source of Anglo-Saxon history – while Alfred was designated in early documents as Rex Anglorum Saxonum, King of the English Saxons.

The Anglo-Saxons meanwhile, had usurped the power of the indigenous Britons – who referred to them as ‘Saeson’ or ‘Saxones.’

It is from this that the Scottish Gaelic term for ‘English people’ of ‘Sasannach’ derives, the Irish Gaelic ‘Sasanach’ and the Welsh ‘Saeson.’

We learn from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle how the religion of the early Anglo-Saxons was one that pre-dated the establishment of Christianity in the British Isles.

Known as a form of Germanic paganism, with roots in Old Norse religion, it shared much in common with the Druidic ‘nature-worshipping’ religion of the indigenous Britons.

It was in the closing years of the sixth century that Christianity began to take a hold in Britain, while by approximately 690 it had become the ‘established’ religion of Anglo-Saxon England.

The first serious shock to Anglo-Saxon control of England came in 789 in the form of sinister black-sailed Viking ships that appeared over the horizon off the island monastery of Lindisfarne, in the northeast of the country.

Lindisfarne was sacked in an orgy of violence and plunder, setting the scene for what would be many more terrifying raids on the coastline of not only England, but also Ireland and Scotland.

But the Vikings, or ‘Northmen’, in common with the Anglo-Saxons of earlier times, were raiders who eventually stayed – establishing, for example, what became Jorvik, or York, and the trading port of Dublin, in Ireland.

Through intermarriage, the bloodlines of the Anglo-Saxons also became infused with that of the Vikings.

But there would be another infusion of the blood of the ‘Northmen’ in the wake of the Norman Conquest of 1066 – a key event in English history that sounded the death knell of Anglo-Saxon supremacy.

By 1066, England had become a nation with several powerful competitors to the throne.

In what were extremely complex family, political and military machinations, the English monarch was Harold II, who had succeeded to the throne following the death of Edward the Confessor.

But his right to the throne was contested by two powerful competitors – his brother-in-law King Harold Hardrada of Norway, in alliance with Tostig, Harold II’s brother, and Duke William II of Normandy.

In what has become known as The Year of Three Battles, Hardrada invaded England and gained victory over the English king on September 20 at the battle of Fulford, in Yorkshire.

Five days later, however, Harold II decisively defeated his brother-in-law and brother at the battle of Stamford Bridge.

But Harold had little time to celebrate his victory, having to immediately march south from Yorkshire to encounter a mighty invasion force, led by Duke William of Normandy that had landed at Hastings, in East Sussex.

Harold’s battle-hardened but exhausted force of Anglo-Saxon soldiers confronted the Normans on October 14 in a battle subsequently depicted on the Bayeux tapestry – a 23ft. long strip of embroidered linen thought to have been commissioned eleven years after the event by the Norman Odo of Bayeux.

It was at the top of Senlac Hill that Harold drew up a strong defensive position, building a shield wall to repel Duke William’s cavalry and infantry.

The Normans suffered heavy losses, but through a combination of the deadly skill of their archers and the ferocious determination of their cavalry they eventually won the day.

Anglo-Saxon morale had collapsed on the battlefield as word spread through the ranks that Harold had been killed – the Bayeux Tapestry depicting this as having happened when the English king was struck by an arrow to the head.

Amidst the carnage of the battlefield, it was difficult to identify Harold – the last of the Anglo-Saxon kings.

Some sources assert William ordered his body to be thrown into the sea, while others state it was secretly buried at Waltham Abbey.

William was declared King of England on December 25, and the complete subjugation of his Anglo-Saxon subjects followed.

Those Normans who had fought on his behalf were rewarded with the lands of Anglo-Saxons, many of whom sought exile abroad as mercenaries.

Within an astonishingly short space of time, Norman manners, customs and law were imposed on England – laying the basis for what subsequently became established ‘English’ custom and practice.

But beneath the surface, old Anglo-Saxon culture was not totally eradicated.

Some aspects were absorbed into those of the Normans, while faint echoes of the Anglo-Saxon past is still seen today in the form of popular surnames such as May.

Honours and distinction

It is in the decades following the Conquest that the May name is first recorded, with one family holding sway as feudal lords of the manor of Faunt, in Sussex.

Subsequent bearers of the name figure prominently in England’s historical record.

Born in 1573, Sir Humphrey May was the politician who, in addition to sitting in the House of Commons from 1605 until a year before his death in 1630, also held for a time the honoured post of Groom of the King’s Privy Chamber under James I (James VI of Scotland.).

An early seventeenth century equivalent of one of today’s ‘celebrity chefs’, Robert May was born in 1588 in Wing, Buckinghamshire.

With his father employed as the chief cook to the wealthy Dormer family of Ascott Park, Buckinghamshire, he was sent by Lady Dormer to train for five years as a chef in Paris.

Returning to Ascott Park, he was later employed by Sir Anthony Browne as his chef at his country estate of Cowdray, in Sussex.

Employed later as chef to a number of other wealthy members of the English aristocracy, it was four years before his death in 1660 that he wrote his famous The Accomplisht Cook, subtitled The Art and Mystery of Cooking.

Recognised as the first major recipe book to be published in England, it is still considered by food experts to be “the most extensive English treatment of potages, broths and soups.”

Also in the vibrancy of seventeenth century England, the oddly but memorably named Baptist May was a courtier during the reign of Charles II.

Born in 1628, a son of Sir Humphrey May, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, it was through the influence of the king’s favourite mistress, Barbara Palmer, Countess of Castlemaine, that he was appointed to the powerful post of Keeper of the Privy Purse.

This was not through any particular regard or love that the beautiful and avaricious Countess of Castlemaine may have held for the unwitting May.

It was to ensure that he, besotted as he was with her, as were many other men, would use the position as keeper of the royal finances to ensure a regular supply of money to herself.

Dismissed from office following the death of Charles II and the accession to the throne of James II, he died in 1698.

He was a cousin of the great English architect Hugh May, born in 1621 and who died in 1684.
